text: Applicability of TDS

Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) is governed by Chapter XVII-B of the Income Tax Act, 1961. However, there are several transactions where no TDS is required to be deducted. These exemptions arise due to specific provisions under the Act, judicial precedents, and clarifications issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT). This paper details transactions where no TDS is applicable along with supporting legal references.

NO TDS under Section 196
In the following cases, tax is not required to be deducted at source:
As per Section 196 of Income tax act, 1961, no deduction of tax shall be made by any person from any sums payable to-
Government (i.e. State and Central Government)
RBI Corporation established under central act which is, under any law for the time being in force, exempt from income-tax on its income, or.
a corporation established by or under a Central Act which is, under any law for the time being in force.
exempt from income-tax on its income Mutual fund specified under section 10(23D).
List of corporations as per TDS section 196(iii) notified as per circular no. 18/2017 issued by CBDT 29th May 2017.

Background: Previous Circulars No. 4/2002 and No. 7/2015 laid down that entities whose income is unconditionally exempt under Section 10 and who are not required to file returns under Section 139 are exempt from TDS. The need to update these circulars to include new entities and remove those whose exemptions have been withdrawn or who are now required to file returns.

This circular ensures that entities whose income is unconditionally exempt and who are not required to file returns are not subjected to TDS, streamlining the process and respecting their tax-exempt status.
No TDS under 194C

Payment of Material – If any sum is required to be paid or credit for carrying out any work relating to manufacturing or supply of product as per the requirement or specification of a customer with the use of material supplied by such customer, tax shall be deducted:
On the invoice value excluding the value of material, if value of material is mentioned separately in the invoice
On the total value of invoice, if value of material is not mentioned separately in the invoice

Transactions in negotiable instruments: The provisions of section 194C would not apply in relation to payments made to banks for discounting bills collecting/receiving payments through cheques/drafts, opening and negotiating Letters of Credit and transactions in negotiable instruments. Case law referred - Associated Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1993] 201 ITR 435. Circular: No. 681, dated 8-3-1994.

Payments to airlines/travel agents: TDS do not apply to the payments made to the airlines or the travel agents for purchase of tickets for air travel of individuals. Circular: No. 713, dated 2-8-1995.

Payments to restaurants/cafes - TDS is not required to be made when payment is made for serving food in a restaurant in the normal course of running of the restaurant/cafe—Circular: No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.

Reimbursement of actual expenses –Sections 194C and 194J refer to any sum paid. Hence, reimbursements cannot be deducted out of the bill amount for the purpose of tax deduction at source. However, where expense are incurred on behalf of another party and the same are merely being reimbursed without raising any separate Invoice, TDS is not applicable.
Case reference:

While reimbursing clearing and forwarding agents amount of freight charges paid by them on behalf of assessee, no TDS liability would arise [CIT v. Opera Global (P.) Ltd. [2014] 52 taxmann.com 299 (Delhi); Sima Agencies v. ITO [2021] 126 taxmann.com 109/279 Taxman 171 (Mad.); Zephyr Biomedicals v. JCIT [2020] 122 taxmann.com 124/[2021] 276 Taxman 305 (Bom.)].

Where seller sold goods to assessee (buyer) and under contract of sale, it was bound to send goods to buyer and to pay transportation charges to goods transport agency and assessee reimbursed freight component to seller and claimed deduction of same, assessee was not liable to deduct tax at source u/s 194C in respect of freight component [Hightension Switchgears (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2016] 71 taxmann.com 207/240 Taxman 582 (Cal.)].

Reimbursement to Employee for Catering Services – The privity of the contract was between the employer (company) and the caterer. The employee acted as a disbursing agent on behalf of the company. The transaction is covered under Section 194C, thus tax withholding under Section 194C is attracted. The reimbursement to the employee should not involve any tax withholding in the hands of employee as it is a cost-only basis repayment.

Octroi collection- Where the assessee was awarded a contract by a municipal committee for collection of octroi, tax is deductible at source on the amount paid to the assessee by the municipal committee, and not on the amount of octroi collected by the assessee [S. S. & Co., Octroi Contractors v. State of Punjab [2004] 268 ITR 398 (P&H)].

Licence fee - Where assessee paid licence fee to IRCTC for granting contract of catering service without deducting tax at source and it has been held that it being a case of payment of licence fee by contractee to contractor, thus, section 194C would not apply [PCIT v. Hakmichand D & Sons [2018] 97 taxmann.com 584/258 Taxman 207 (SC)]

Damages - Amount paid by sub-contractor to main contractor on account of extra costs that main contractor had to incur due to delay in completion of work by sub-contractor was not liable to TDS u/s 194C [CIT v. Karnavati Infrastructure (P.) Ltd. [2015] 54 taxmann.com 246/229 Taxman 241 (Guj.)].

Minimum guarantee payments - Where assessee entered into merchant agreement with various hotels for facilitating reservation/booking of hotel rooms through platform of assessee, however, assessee was merely compensating shortfall pursuant to agreement and no work had been carried out, therefore, assessee would not be liable for TDS under section 194C on minimum guarantee payments made to hotels. [Oravel Stays (P.) Ltd. v. Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax, Special Range-7, [2024] 159 taxmann.com 423 (Delhi - Trib.)]

External development charges (EDC) paid by assessee-society to development authority (GMADA), as per policy decision of government and not out of contractual obligations, would not attract section 194C. [Punjab IAS & PCS Officers House Building Society Ltd. v. Income-tax Officer, [2024] 158 taxmann.com 293 (Chandigarh - Trib.)]

Contract Manufacturing on principal-to-principal basis: mere specifications-oriented manufacturing does not vitiate the nature of the contract for sale. If the contract manufacturer supplies goods to ICo on a principal-to-principal basis, where the title in the goods passes to ICo on delivery, Section 194C would not apply.
No tds under 194J
Illustrative transactions:

TDS on Service tax/ GST- TDS is not applicable on Service tax or any other Indirect component. The Board had issued a Circular No. 4/2008, dated 28-4-2008. Further, any reference to 'service tax' in an existing agreement or contract which was entered prior to 1-7-2017 shall he treated as 'GST on services' with respect to the period from 1-7-2017 onward till the expiry of such agreement or contract. - Circular No. 23/2017, dated 19-7-2017.

Mobile data utilisation - Payment made by assessee, a mobile service provider company, to another mobile service provider Company for utilization of roaming mobile data and connectivity could not be termed as technical service [CIT v. Vodafone South Ltd. [2016] 72 taxmann.com 347/241 Taxman 497 (Kar.), followed in CIT v. Tata Teleservices Ltd. [2022] 142 taxmann.com 51/288 Taxman 775 (Delhi)]. Services rendered by MTNL/other companies via interconnect/port access cannot be regarded as technical services as contemplated by section 194J [CIT v. Bharti Cellular Ltd. [2008] 175 Taxman 573 (Delhi)].

Telephone services - When a person decides to subscribe to a cellular telephone service in order to have the facility of being able to communicate with others, he does not contract to receive a technical service. What he does agree is to pay for the use of the airtime for which he pays a charge. What applies to cellular mobile telephone is also applicable to fixed telephone service. Neither service can be regarded as 'technical service' for the purpose of section 194J [Skycell Communications Ltd. v. DCIT [2001] 119 Taxman 496/251 ITR 53 (Mad.)].

Stock exchange service - Services made available by Bombay Stock Exchange [BSE Online Trading (BOLT) System] for which transaction charges are paid by members of BSE are common services that every member of Stock Exchange is necessarily required to avail of to carry out trading in securities in stock exchange; such services do not amount to 'technical services' provided by stock exchange, not being services specifically sought for by user or consumer and, therefore, no TDS would be deductible u/s 194J on payments made for such services [CIT v. Kotak Securities Ltd. [2016] 67 taxmann.com 356/239 Taxman 139 (SC)].
No tds under 194H

Turnover Commission payable by RBI to Agency Banks - Requirement of tax deduction at source under section 194H is not applicable in respect of Turnover Commission payable by the Reserve Bank of India to the Agency Banks (Banks authorized for conducting Government business) for performing the general banking business of the Central and State Governments on behalf of RBI - Circular : No. 6/2003, dated 3-9-2003.

Credit card purchases - Commission to bank on payments received from customers who had made purchases through credit cards is not liable to TDS [CIT v. JSD Apparels (P.) Ltd. [2015] 53 taxmann.com 139 (Delhi)].

Debit/ Credit card charges: Tax is not required to be deducted under S. 194H on the debit/credit card charges. This supported by judicial precedents and Notification No. 56/2012 dated 31 December 2012 issued by Central Government.

Trade Discounts & Sales Incentives: In Gujarat Tea Processors & Packers Ltd. v. DCIT [2012] 28 taxmann.com 187 (Guj.), it was held that trade discounts given by a manufacturer/seller to a retailer under a sales promotion scheme do not attract TDS under Section 194H as they do not constitute commission.

Trade discount given by newspaper agencies to advertising agencies working for advertisers is not in nature of commission [Jagran Prakashan Ltd. v. DCIT [2012] 21 taxmann.com 489/209 Taxman 92 (All.); PCIT v. Dempo Industries (P.) Ltd. [2021] 126 taxmann.com 112/279 Taxman 166 (Bom.)].

Del Credere Agents & Retailer Incentives: In CIT v. United Breweries Ltd. [2017] 80 taxmann.com 123 (AP & Telangana), the High Court ruled that trade incentives paid by an assessee to retailers through del credere agents for boosting sales did not qualify as commission since there was no principal-agent relationship between the assessee and the retailers. Consequently, TDS under Section 194H was not applicable.

Principal-to-Principal Transactions & Temporary Incentives: In National Panasonic India (P) Ltd. v. DCIT (2005) 94 TTJ 899 (Delhi Tribunal), the Tribunal examined whether incentives paid to dealers constituted "commission" under Section 194H. The court ruled that since the relationship between the parties was on a principal-to-principal basis, such payments were not commission but promotional incentives. The incentive schemes were temporary, sales-driven, and not a permanent feature of the business relationship, meaning TDS under Section 194H was not applicable.

Guarantee commission - Payment of guarantee commission made by assessee to banks was not covered under 'commission or brokerage' [CIT v. Nimbus Communications Ltd. [2019] 109 taxmann.com 498/266 Taxman 375 (SC)].

Payment gateway facility charges - Where assessee, which was selling travel products, paid fees to banks for providing payment gateway facility, same could not be treated as commission or brokerage, hence, not liable to tax u/s 194H [PCIT v. Make My Trip India (P.) Ltd. [2019] 104 taxmann.com 263/263 Taxman 271 (Delhi)]. Service charges paid by assessee bank to National Financial Switch and Cash Tree for routing transactions of payments made by customers of assessee-bank to acquiring bank would not be liable to TDS deduction u/s 194H [CIT v. Corporation Bank [2021] 123 taxmann.com 204/277 Taxman 207 (Kar.); CIT v. Karnataka Bank Ltd. [2022] 142 taxmann.com 64 (Karn.), SLP granted in CIT v. Karnataka Bank Ltd. [2022] 142 taxmann.com 65/288 Taxman 725 (SC)].
No tds under 194I

Income received by certain defence funds - In respect of any income received by any person on behalf of any Regimental Fund or Non-public Fund established by the Armed Forces of the Union for the welfare of past and present members of such forces or their defendants, no tax may be deducted at source under section 194-I, since the income of these organisations is exempt from tax under section 10(23AA)—Circular : No. 735, dated 30-1-1996.

Non-applicability of provisions of section 194-I on remittance of Passenger Service Fees (PSF) by an airline to an airport operator-  The Board has accepted the above view of the High Court of Bombay. Accordingly, it is now a settled position that section 194-I of the Act, will not apply on PSF.

Wheeling/transmission charges - Wheeling or transmission charges paid to power transmitting companies by assessee-electricity distribution company did not amount to 'rent' requiring TDS u/s 194-I [CIT v. Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. [2015] 58 taxmann.com 339/232 Taxman 373, SLP dismissed in CIT v. Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. [2016] 74 taxmann.com 8/242 Taxman 369 (SC)].

TDS Section – 194H
Applicability
Section 194H of the Income Tax Act, 1961, deals with the deduction of Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on income earned as commission or brokerage.

Any Person other than an individual or Hindu undivided family is required to deduct tax us 194H. Individual or Hindu undivided family will be required to deduct if total Sales/gross receipts/turnover from business exceeds 1 crore Rupees or if total gross receipts from profession exceeds 50 lakh Rupees.
Commission or brokerage
Meaning of Commission or brokerage as per TDS section 194H

"Commission or brokerage" refers to any payment, whether direct or indirect, received by a person acting on behalf of another for non-professional services, facilitating the buying or selling of goods, or assisting in transactions involving assets, valuable articles, or things (excluding securities).

The expression "professional services" means services rendered by a person in the course of carrying on a legal, medical, engineering or architectural profession or the profession of accountancy or technical consultancy or interior decoration or such other profession as is notified by the Board for the purposes of section 44AA;

The expression "securities" mentioned above shall have the meaning assigned to it in clause (h) of section 2 of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 (42 of 1956). Definition of Securities reproduced below:
Securities include:
shares, scrips, stocks, bonds, debentures, debenture stock or other marketable securities of a like nature in or of any incorporated company or other body corporate;
(ia) derivative;
(ib) units or any other instrument issued by any collective investment scheme to the investors in such schemes;
(ic) security receipt as defined in clause (zg) of section 2 of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002;
(id) units or any other such instrument issued to the investors under any mutual fund scheme;
Explanation,

For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that "securities" shall not include any unit linked insurance policy or scrips or any such instrument or unit, by whatever name called, which provides a combined benefit risk on the life of the persons and investment by such persons and issued by an insurer referred to in clause (9) of section 2 of the Insurance Act, 1938 (4 of 1938);
Rate of Tax
Payment to Resident- Applicable Tax rate for transaction upto 01 Oct 24 is 5%, post 01 Oct 24 applicable TDS rate is reduced to 2%.
Payment to Non Resident- TDS will apply as per section 195
Payment by Individual/ HUF (who are not required to deduct TDS us.194H)- TDS will apply as per section 194N
Insurance Commission to Insurance Broker: TDS will apply as per section 194D
Exemption from the section
Any commission/brokerage payable to Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited or Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Limited

By virtue of Section 196, no tax shall be deducted under this provision from any sum payable to the Govt., RBI, Mutual Fund or any Corporation established under a central Act which is exempt from paying income-tax.
Insurance commission paid/payable under section 194D of the Act
Important Points

The word “acting on behalf” used in the explanation bolsters the view that this section is invoked only when there is a principal-agent relation between the transacting parties. This proposition has been upheld by plethora of judgements as well as by the apex court.

Although, the term agent is not defined anywhere in the Act but post reading and understanding of these judicial precedents as well as Indian Contract Act, 1872, following factors becomes relevant for examining the agency relationship:

An agent is employed to make bargains and contracts for compensation; a middleman or negotiator between parties; an agent of a buyer or a seller who buys or sells stocks, bonds, commodities, or services, usually on a commission basis;
The agent makes the principal answerable to third persons whereby the principal can sue third parties directly and renders himself liable to be sued directly by the third parties;

The person, who purports to enter into a transaction on behalf of the principal, would have the power to create, modify or terminate contractual relationship between his principal, that is, the person whom he represents, and the third parties;

An agent, though bound by instructions given to him by the principal does not work under the direct control and supervision of the principal. The agent, thus, uses his own discretion to act on behalf of the principal, subject to the limits to his authority prescribed by the principal;
There is no necessity of a formal contract of agency; it can be implied which can arise from the act of parties or situations in which parties are put.

The use of “commission/brokerage” as a nomenclature for payment and dealing between parties is not enough for triggering WHT implications under this section. The payment is in fact, commission/brokerage or not depends on the facts and circumstances of the case and the conduct between parties.

Though commission is typically determined on the value of goods/services, still the manner of calculation of commission or the manner of payment of commission may not be always relevant for examining WHT implications.
Illustrative transactions:

Turnover Commission payable by RBI to Agency Banks - Requirement of tax deduction at source under section 194H is not applicable in respect of Turnover Commission payable by the Reserve Bank of India to the Agency Banks (Banks authorized for conducting Government business) for performing the general banking business of the Central and State Governments on behalf of RBI - Circular : No. 6/2003, dated 3-9-2003.

Commission/ Supplementary commission received by travel agents – The Supreme Court in Singapore Airlines Ltd. v. CIT [2022] 144 taxmann.com 221 / [2023] 290 Taxman 139 (SC) upheld the ruling of the Delhi High Court, affirming that supplementary commission earned by travel agents over and above the net fare is subject to TDS under Section 194H. The airline had agreements with travel agents who sold tickets on its behalf and earned payments in two forms—standard commission (subject to TDS) and supplementary commission (not subjected to TDS by the airline). The key issue was whether this additional commission retained by travel agents constituted "commission" under Section 194H, thereby attracting a TDS obligation on the airline.

The court held that Section 194H applies to both direct and indirect commission payments, irrespective of their mode or source. The relationship between the airline and travel agents was that of principal and agent under Section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, confirming that the supplementary commission was part of the overall agency arrangement. Since this additional amount was earned in connection with ticket sales and was known to the airline, it could not be classified as a mere discount. The Supreme Court ruled that the airline was required to deduct TDS on the supplementary commission, reinforcing the principle that any earnings by an agent arising from an agency relationship, whether received directly or indirectly, are subject to TDS under Section 194H.

In the case of Around the World Travels & Tours (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2004] 141 Taxman 53 (Mad.), it was held that tax should be deducted at source under section 194H on amount available to agents being difference between airfare fixed by Airlines and price at which agents are enabled to sell tickets.

Payments by television channels and publishing houses to advertisement companies for procuring or canvassing for advertisements - The issue of applicability of TDS provisions on payments made by television channels or media houses publishing newspapers or magazines to advertising agencies for procuring and canvassing for advertisements has been examined by the Board.
It is noted that there are two types of payments involved in the advertising business:
Payment by client to the advertising agency, and
Payment by advertising agency to the television channel/newspaper company

The applicability of TDS on these payments has already been dealt with in Circular No. 715 dated 8-8-1995, where it has been clarified in Question Nos. 1 & 2 that while TDS under section 194C (as work contract) will be applicable on the first type of payment, there will be no TDS under section 194C on the second type of payment e.g. payment by advertising agency to the media company.

However, another issue has been raised in various cases as to whether the fees/charges taken or retained by advertising companies from media companies for canvassing/booking advertisements (typically 15% of the billing) is 'commission' or 'discount'. It has been argued by the assessees that since the relationship between the media company and the advertising company is on a principal-to-principal basis, such payments are in the nature of trade discount and not commission and, therefore, outside the purview of TDS under section 194H. The Department, on the other hand, has taken the stand in some cases that since the advertising agencies act on behalf of the media companies for procuring advertisements, the margin retained by the former amounts to constructive payment of commission and, accordingly, TDS under section 194H is attracted.

The issue has been examined by the Allahabad High Court in the case of Jagran Prakashan Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2015] 56 taxmann.com 208 and Delhi High Court in the matter of Living Media Limited and it was held in both the cases that the relationship between the media company and the advertising agency is that of a 'principal-to-principal' and, therefore, not liable for TDS under section 194H. The SLPs filed by the Department in the matter of Living Media Ltd. and Jagran Prakashan Ltd. have been dismissed by the Supreme Court vide order dated 11-12-2009 and order dated 5-5-2014, respectively. Though these decisions are in respect of print media, the ratio is also applicable to electronic media/television advertising as the broad nature of the activities involved is similar.

In view of the above, it is hereby clarified that no TDS is attracted on payments made by television channels/newspaper companies to the advertising agency for booking or procuring of or canvassing for advertisements. It is also further clarified that 'commission' referred to in Question No. 27 of the Board's Circular No. 715 dated 8-8-1995 does not refer to payments by media companies to advertising companies for booking of advertisements but to payments for engagement of models, artists, photographers, sportspersons, etc. and, therefore, is not relevant to the issue of TDS referred to in this Circular.—Circular No. 5/2016, dated 29-2-2016.

Commission paid to agencies - Section 194H would be applicable to payments made by assessee, a Government organization running TV channel called 'Doordarshan', to advertising agencies to secure more business as these were in nature of commission paid to agencies [Director, Prasar Bharati v. CIT [2018] 92 taxmann.com 11/255 Taxman 1 (SC)].

Credit card purchases - Commission to bank on payments received from customers who had made purchases through credit cards is not liable to TDS [CIT v. JSD Apparels (P.) Ltd. [2015] 53 taxmann.com 139 (Delhi)].
Trade Discounts & Sales Incentives:

In Gujarat Tea Processors & Packers Ltd. v. DCIT [2012] 28 taxmann.com 187 (Guj.), it was held that trade discounts given by a manufacturer/seller to a retailer under a sales promotion scheme do not attract TDS under Section 194H as they do not constitute commission.

Trade discount given by newspaper agencies to advertising agencies working for advertisers is not in nature of commission [Jagran Prakashan Ltd. v. DCIT [2012] 21 taxmann.com 489/209 Taxman 92 (All.); PCIT v. Dempo Industries (P.) Ltd. [2021] 126 taxmann.com 112/279 Taxman 166 (Bom.)].

However, in Tube Investments of India Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2009] 223 CTR (Mad.) 99, the Tribunal held that where dealers sold goods at the same price at which they were purchased from the manufacturer, the trade incentive provided to them constituted commission within the meaning of Section 194H and was thus subject to TDS
Bulk Purchase Discounts:

In CIT v. Ahmedabad Stamp Vendors Association [2012] 25 taxmann.com 201 (SC), the Supreme Court held that the discount allowed to stamp vendors on bulk purchases was in the nature of a cash discount arising from a principal-to-principal transaction of sale and, therefore, was not liable to TDS under Section 194H.
Del Credere Agents & Retailer Incentives:

In CIT v. United Breweries Ltd. [2017] 80 taxmann.com 123 (AP & Telangana), the High Court ruled that trade incentives paid by an assessee to retailers through del credere agents for boosting sales did not qualify as commission since there was no principal-agent relationship between the assessee and the retailers. Consequently, TDS under Section 194H was not applicable.
Discounts to Third-Party Collection Centres:

In CIT v. Super Religare Laboratories Ltd. [2021] 133 taxmann.com 313 (Bom.), the Bombay High Court held that where an assessee engaged in laboratory and testing services allowed discounts to third-party collection centres, but did not make direct payments to them, there was no TDS obligation under Section 194H. The Supreme Court later issued an SLP notice in CIT v. Super Religare Laboratories Ltd. [2022] 139 taxmann.com 369 (SC), keeping the matter open for further consideration.

Principal-agent relationship - Assessee had appointed a large number of agents to sell its milk and milk products from booths owned by it. Commission was being paid to agents for milk sold and unsold milk was taken back by assessee at same price. Cash collection was daily handed over to assessee by agents. Since there was principal to agent relationship and, thus, assessee was liable to deduct tax at source on commission paid by it [Delhi Milk Scheme v. CIT [2008] 173 Taxman 54 (Delhi)]. However, commission paid by Mother Dairy to concessionaires who sell milk of assessee from booths owned by assessee not liable to TDS [CIT v. Mother Dairy India Ltd. [2012] 18 taxmann.com 49/206 Taxman 157 (Delhi)].
Principal-to-principal transaction -

Where assessee-airlines issued tickets to its travel agents at a concessional price, transaction between assessee and travel agents was that of principal-to-principal and difference in price was discount, therefore, such transaction would not fall within the ambit of section 194H [CIT v. Singapore Airlines Ltd. [2009] 180 Taxman 128 (Delhi)]. Also see, CIT v. Jai Drinks (P.) Ltd. [2011] 10 taxmann.com 115/198 Taxman 271 (Delhi). Where assessee paid target incentives to dealers for increasing sales of its products, since there was no relationship of principal and agent between assessee and distributors, assessee was not required to deduct tax at source u/s 194H while making said payments [PCIT v. Shalimar Chemical Works Ltd. [2018] 96 taxmann.com 275/257 Taxman 590 (Cal.)].

In National Panasonic India (P) Ltd. v. DCIT (2005) 94 TTJ 899 (Delhi Tribunal), the Tribunal examined whether incentives paid to dealers constituted "commission" under Section 194H. The court ruled that since the relationship between the parties was on a principal-to-principal basis, such payments were not commission but promotional incentives. The incentive schemes were temporary, sales-driven, and not a permanent feature of the business relationship, meaning TDS under Section 194H was not applicable.

Similarly, in Ahmedabad Stamp Vendors Association v. UOI (2012) 82 CCH 210 ISSC, upheld by the Supreme Court, it was held that to attract TDS under Section 194H, an agency relationship must exist. A mere discount on pricing by a seller does not amount to commission within the meaning of Section 194H.

Benefits/ Perquisites to Doctor - Where assessee-pharmaceutical company incurred expenses for providing services such as taxi services, booking of air-tickets, cost of souvenir, etc., for conferences of doctors, in view of the fact that these doctors were not bound to prescribe medicines as suggested by assessee and, therefore, there existed no agency relationship between assessee and doctors, said expenses incurred by assessee for doctors could not be treated as commission liable to TDS u/s 194H [CIT v. Intas Pharmaceuticals Ltd. [2021] 129 taxmann.com 347/283 Taxman 215 (Guj.), SLP notice issued in CIT v. Intas Pharmaceuticals Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 455/286 Taxman 560 (SC)].

Guarantee commission - Payment of guarantee commission made by assessee to banks was not covered under 'commission or brokerage' [CIT v. Nimbus Communications Ltd. [2019] 109 taxmann.com 498/266 Taxman 375 (SC)].

Payment gateway facility charges - Where assessee, which was selling travel products, paid fees to banks for providing payment gateway facility, same could not be treated as commission or brokerage, hence, not liable to tax u/s 194H [PCIT v. Make My Trip India (P.) Ltd. [2019] 104 taxmann.com 263/263 Taxman 271 (Delhi)]. Service charges paid by assessee bank to National Financial Switch and Cash Tree for routing transactions of payments made by customers of assessee-bank to acquiring bank would not be liable to TDS deduction u/s 194H [CIT v. Corporation Bank [2021] 123 taxmann.com 204/277 Taxman 207 (Kar.); CIT v. Karnataka Bank Ltd. [2022] 142 taxmann.com 64 (Karn.), SLP granted in CIT v. Karnataka Bank Ltd. [2022] 142 taxmann.com 65/288 Taxman 725 (SC)].

Reimbursement of commission expenses- Tax is not to be deducted u/s 194H on reimbursement of commission expenses which was paid by another company on behalf of assessee [CIT v. Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd. [2018] 92 taxmann.com 30/254 Taxman 370 (Bom.), SLP dismissed in CIT v. Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 533/269 Taxman 569 (SC)].

Discount coupons/ Recharge coupons - Sale of SIM cards/recharge coupons at discounted rate to distributors is not commission and, therefore, not liable to TDS u/s 194H [CIT v. Idea Cellular Ltd. [2021] 125 taxmann.com 171 (Bom.), SLP granted in CIT v. Idea Cellular Ltd. [2021] 125 taxmann.com 172/278 Taxman 188 (SC); CIT v. Vodafone Cellular Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 191 (Bom.); SLP granted in CIT v. Vodafone Cellular Ltd. [2023] 146 taxmann.com 282 (SC)]. However, in CIT v. Idea Cellular Ltd. [2010] 189 Taxman 118 (Delhi), it has been held that discount given by assessee, a mobile cellular operator, to distributors in course of selling of sim cards and recharge coupons under prepaid scheme of getting a connection is, in substance, a payment for services to be rendered by distributors to assessee and, so much so, it would fall within definition of commission or brokerage [Vodafone Essar Cellular Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2010] 194 Taxman 518 (Ker.)].

Sale or return arrangement between manufacturer and retailer- The issue under consideration is whether the arrangement between ABC (manufacturer) and PQR (retailer) under a Sales with Right to Return (SOR) model qualifies as a Principal-to-Principal (P2P) or Principal-to-Agent (P2A) relationship, thereby determining the applicability of TDS under Section 194H on the margin earned by PQR. In this scenario, the actual legal nature of the transaction needs to be determined based on various factors, few of which are provided below.
Exclusivity: PQR is not an exclusive dealer and can stock competing products.
Privity of contract: The end customer deals solely with PQR, and ABC has no direct contractual obligation toward them.
Title transfer: Legal ownership of goods momentarily vests with PQR at the time of sale to the end customer.
Pricing discretion: PQR has the autonomy to sell at a price lower than the MRP, designing its own discounts.
Credit risk: PQR bears the credit risk for any sales made on a credit basis.
Based on these factors and facts of current case, the transaction appears to be a P2P arrangement, suggesting that TDS under Section 194H may not be applicable on the margin earned by PQR.

Domestic Money Transfer (DMT) business model:  A Co facilitates money transfers through a prepaid wallet system, where funds are digitally transferred between retailers, distributors, and A Co without actual cash movement. Initially, A Co argued that no TDS was deductible as there was no direct payment to the distributor, relying on the principle that TDS applies only where payment is made.

Yes, TDS under Section 194H is applicable on the commission/service fees paid by A Co to its distributors. This is based on the reasoning that the margin retained by distributors is considered as commission for facilitating the Domestic Money Transfer (DMT) service. Judicial precedents (such as CIT v. Idea Cellular Ltd. and CIT v. Singapore Airlines Ltd.) have established that even if no direct payment is made, TDS is applicable on the commission component.

Debit/ Credit card charges: Tax is not required to be deducted under S. 194H on the debit/credit card charges. This supported by judicial precedents and Notification No. 56/2012 dated 31 December 2012 issued by Central Government.

Facilitate sale of goods transaction for E-commerce participant: The issue under consideration is whether TDS under Section 194H applies to the commission retained by A Co. while facilitating e-commerce transactions on its platform, despite tax already being deducted under Section 194-O. A Co. operates an e-commerce platform where a third-party manufacturer (TPM) sells products, and A Co. retains a 3% commission before remitting the sale proceeds to TPM after deducting TDS under Section 194-O. The primary question is whether this commission should be subjected to additional TDS under Section 194H or whether Section 194-O(3), which prevents double TDS on the same transaction, provides an exemption.

Upon analysis, it is concluded that Section 194-O(3) does not exempt the commission from TDS under Section 194H because there are two separate transactions: (1) the payment of sale proceeds by A Co. to TPM (subject to TDS under Section 194-O) and (2) the commission retained by A Co. for using its platform (which is an income for A Co.). Since Section 194-O(3) applies to the same transaction and does not cover distinct transactions, the commission retained by A Co. qualifies as a commission payment under Section 194H. Thus, TPM is required to deduct TDS at 5% under Section 194H on the commission retained by A Co.

Discount on sale of set top boxes: The issue under consideration is whether the discount given on the sale of Set-Top Boxes (STBs), Recharge Coupon Vouchers (RCVs), and Starter Kits (SKs) to distributors qualifies as commission under Section 194H of the Income Tax Act, thereby attracting TDS liability. The tax authorities argue that the principal-agent relationship exists between the company (PQR) and its distributors, and the difference between MRP and the distributor price is commission rather than a trade discount. Conversely, PQR contends that the transactions are on a Principal-to-Principal (P2P) basis, where ownership and risks transfer to the distributor at the time of sale, thus Section 194H should not apply.

TDS Section – 194J
Scope / Coverage / Non-Coverage:
Section 194J provides for deduction of tax at source payable to a resident by way of:
Threshold limit for withholding of tax on fees for professional services

If aggregate of the amounts of such sums credited or paid or likely to be credited or likely to be paid during the financial year to the account of, or to, the payee, does not exceed INR 30,000/- then the liability of withholding of tax does not arise.
Fees for professional services
Meaning of ‘Professional services’ under 194J(1)(a)
Professional services under section 194J(1)(a) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 mean professional services rendered by a person in the course of carrying on following professions:

Legal profession, Medical profession, Engineering profession, Architectural profession, Profession of accountancy, Profession of technical consultancy, Profession of interior decoration, or profession of advertising; and

Services rendered by a person in the course of carrying on profession as notified by the CBDT for the purpose of section 44AA or section 194J. The CDBT has so far notified following profession for the sections 44AA and section 194J:

Authorized representative - A person who represents any other person, on payment of any fee or remuneration before any tribunal or authority constituted or appointed by or under any law for the time being in force, but does not include an employee of the person so represented or a person carrying on legal profession or a person carrying on the profession of accountancy.

Film artist i.e., any person engaged in his professional capacity in the production of a cinematograph film, whether produced by him or by any other person, as — an actor, a cameraman, a director including an assistant director, a music director including an assistant music director, an art director including an assistant art director, a dance director including an assistant dance director, an editor, a singer, a lyricist, a story writer, a screenplay writer, a dialogue writer; and dress designer.

Profession of company secretary - For this purpose, a company secretary means a person who is a member of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India in practice within the meaning of section 2(2) of the Company Secretaries Act, 1980.
Profession of information technology
Following Sports Persons - Umpires and Referees; Coaches and Trainers; Team Physicians and Physiotherapists; Event Managers; Commentators; Anchors; Sports Columnist
Fees for technical services (‘FTS’) – Section 194J(1)(b)
Meaning of Technical services as per the Income-tax Act, 1961

Technical services means any consideration including any lump sum consideration for the rendering of any managerial, technical or consultancy services (including the provision of services of technical or other personnel) but does not include consideration for any construction, assembly, and mining or like project undertaken by the recipient or consideration which would be income of the recipient chargeable under the head "Salaries".
Royalty as per Section 194J(1)(c)
"Royalty" means consideration (including any lump sum consideration but excluding any consideration which would be the income of the recipient chargeable under the head "Capital gains") for:
The transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a license) in respect of a patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trademark or similar property;
The imparting of any information concerning the working of, or the use of, a patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trademark or similar property;
The use of any patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trademark or similar property;
The imparting of any information concerning technical, industrial, commercial or scientific knowledge, experience or skill;
The use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment;

The transfer of all or any rights (including the granting of a license) in respect of any copyright, literary, artistic or scientific work including films or video tapes for use in connection with television or tapes for use in connection with radio broadcasting.
Explanations:
"Computer software" means any computer programme recorded on any disc, tape, perforated media or other information storage device and includes any such programme or any customized electronic data.

Transfer of all or any rights in respect of any right, property or information includes and has always included transfer of all or any right for use or right to use a computer software (including granting of a licence) irrespective of the medium through which such right is transferred.
Royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not:
the possession or control of such right, property or information is with the payer;
such right, property or information is used directly by the payer;
the location of such right, property or information is in India.

“Process" includes and shall be deemed to have always included transmission by satellite (including up-linking, amplification, conversion for down-linking of any signal), cable, optic fibre or by any other similar technology, whether or not such process is secret.
Non-compete fees- 194J(1)(d)

Section 194J(1)(d) covers list of services covered under clause (va) of section 28. Clause (va) of section 28, provides following sum, whether received or receivable, in cash or kind, under an agreement as income from business or profession:—
For not carrying out any activity in relation to any business; or

For not sharing any know-how, patent, copyright, trade mark, license, franchise or any other business or commercial right of similar nature or information or technique likely to assist in the manufacture or processing of goods or provision for services, but excluding any sum, whether received or receivable, in cash or kind, on account of transfer of the right to manufacture, produce or process any article or thing or right to carry on any business, which is chargeable under the head 'Capital gains';

Any sum received as compensation, from the multilateral fund of the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone layer under the United Nations Environment Programme, in accordance with the terms of agreement entered into with the Government of India.
For the purposes of clause (va) of section 28,
'Agreement' includes any arrangement or understanding or action in concert,-
Whether or not such arrangement, understanding or action is formal or in writing; or
Whether or not such arrangement, understanding or action is intended to be enforceable by legal proceedings;

'service' means service of any description which is made available to potential users and includes the provision of services in connection with business of any industrial or commercial nature such as accounting, banking, communication, conveying of news or information, advertising, entertainment, amusement, education, financing, insurance, chit funds, real estate, construction, transport, storage, processing, supply of electrical or other energy, boarding and lodging.
Dictionary meanings of Phrases used in section
Illustrative transactions covered under jurisprudence:

Payments by advertising agency to artistes - When an advertising agency makes payments for professional services to a film artiste such as an actor, a cameraman, a director, etc., tax will be deducted at the rate of 5 per cent—Circular: No. 714, dated 3-8-1995/Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.
Clarifications on payments to certain institutions/agencies - The following clarifications are issued:
- Payments to recruitment agencies are in the nature of payments for services rendered, and hence will be subject to TDS under section 194J of the Act, and not under section 194C of the Act.
- Payments made by a company to a share registrar will also similarly be liable to tax deduction at source under section 194J and not under section 194C.

- In respect of payment of commission to external parties for procuring orders for the company's products, rendering of such services is not covered under section 194C, but may involve payment of fees for professional or technical services, in which case tax may be deductible under section 194J.
- Payments made to a hospital for rendering medical services will attract deduction of tax at source under section 194J.
- Commission received by the advertising agency from the media would require deduction of tax at source under section 194J.

- Routine/normal maintenance contracts which include supply of spares will be covered under section 194C. However, where technical services are rendered, the provisions of section 194J will apply in regard to tax deduction at source.
- Since section 194J refers to 'any sum paid', reimbursement of actual expenses cannot be deducted out of the bill amount for the purpose of tax deduction at source.
Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.

Fees received from abroad - In respect of fees for professional services received from foreign companies or foreign law and accountancy firms, any fees paid through regular banking channels to any chartered accountant, lawyer, advocate or solicitor who is resident in India by non-residents who do not have any agent or business connection or permanent establishment in India may not be subjected to deduction of tax at source under section 194J. However, foreign companies or foreign law and accountancy firms are required to send a quarterly statement, indicating the name and address of the persons to whom the payments are made, to the CBDT—Circular : No. 726, dated 18-10-1995.

Vide Circular No. 766, dated 24-4-1998, it is clarified that as the details of payments made to the Indian residents can easily be verified or collected wherever required, it has been decided to discontinue with immediate effect the requirement of sending the above quarterly statements.

Deduction to be made under one section only - In some cases persons responsible for deducting tax at source are deducting such tax by applying more than one provisions for the same payment. In particular, it has been pointed out that the sums paid for carrying out work of advertising are being subjected to deduction of tax at source under section 194C as payment for work contract as also under section 194J as payments of fees for professional services.

The Board has clarified that each section, regarding TDS under Chapter XVII, deals with a particular kind of payment to the exclusion of all other sections in this Chapter. Thus, payment of any sum shall be liable for deduction of tax only under one section. Therefore, a payment is liable for tax deduction only under one section—Circular : No. 720, dated 30-8-1995.

TDS on service tax component- TDS is not applicable on Service tax component. The Board had issued a Circular No. 4/2008, dated 28-4-2008 wherein it was clarified that tax is to be deducted at source under section 194-I of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (hereafter referred to as 'the Act'), on the amount of rent paid/payable without including the service tax component. Representations/letters has been received seeking clarification whether such principle can be extended to other provisions of the Act also.

2. Attention of CBDT has also been drawn to the judgment of the Hon'ble Rajasthan High Court dated 1-7-2013, in the case of CIT (TDS) Jaipur v. Rajasthan Urban Infrastructure (Income-tax Appeal Nos. 235, 222, 238 and 239/2011), holding that if as per the terms of the agreement between the payer and the payee, the amount of service tax is to be paid separately and was not included in the fees for professional services or technical services, no TDS is required to be made on the service tax component under section 194J of the Act.

3. The matter has been examined afresh. In exercise of the powers conferred under section 119 of the Act, the Board has decided that wherever in terms of the agreement/contract between the payer and the payee, the service tax component comprised in the amount payable to a resident is indicated separately, tax shall be deducted at source under Chapter XVII-B of the Act on the amount paid/payable without including such service tax component.—Circular No. 1/2014, dated 13-1-2014.

Substitution of Service Tax by Goods and Services Tax (GST) – TDS is not available on GST component. The Central Board of Direct Taxes ('the Board') had earlier issued Circular No. 1/2014, dated 13-1-2014 clarifying that wherever in terms of the agreement or contract between the payer and the payee, the Service Tax component comprised in the amount payable to a resident is indicated separately, tax shall be deducted at source under Chapter XVII-B of the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act') on the amount paid or payable without including such Service Tax component.

2. References have been received in the Board seeking clarification as to what treatment would be required to be given to the component of Goods and Services Tax (GST) on services, which has been introduced by the Government with effect from 1st of July, 2017 and into which the erstwhile Service Tax has been subsumed.

3. The matter has been examined. It is noted that the Government has brought in force a new Goods and Services Tax regime with effect from 1-7-2017 replacing, amongst others, the Service Tax which was being charged prior to this date as per the provisions of Finance Act, 1994. Therefore, there is a need to harmonize the contents of Circular No. 1/2014 of the Board with the new system for taxation of services under the GST regime.

4. In the light of the fact that even under the new GST regime, the rationale of excluding the tax component from the purview of TDS remains valid, the Board hereby clarifies that wherever in terms of the agreement or contract between the payer and the payee, the component of 'GST on services' comprised in the amount payable to a resident is indicated separately, tax shall be deducted at source under Chapter XVII-B of the Act on the amount paid or payable without including such 'GST on services' component. GST for these purposes shall include Integrated Goods and Services Tax, Central Goods and Services Tax, State Goods and Services Tax and Union Territory Goods and Services Tax.

5. For the purposes of this Circular, any reference to 'service tax' in an existing agreement or contract which was entered prior to 1-7-2017 shall he treated as 'GST on services' with respect to the period from 1-7-2017 onward till the expiry of such agreement or contract. - Circular No. 23/2017, dated 19-7-2017.

Notified professional services u/s 194J, Explanation (a) - In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (a) of the Explanation to section 194J of the Income-tax Act, 1961, Central Board of Direct Taxes hereby notifies the services rendered by following persons in relation to the sports activities as "Professional Services" for the purpose of the said section, namely : Sports Persons, Umpires and Referees, Coaches and Trainers, Team Physicians and Physiotherapists, Event Managers, Commentators, Anchors and Sports Columnists.
2. This notification shall come into force with effect from the date of its publication in the Official Gazette - Notification No. S.O. 2085(E), dated 21-8-2008.

Third Party Administrators (TPAs) with hospitals etc. - The services rendered by hospitals to various patients are primarily medical services and, therefore, provisions of section 194J are applicable on payments made by TPAs to hospitals etc. Further for invoking provisions of section 194J, there is no stipulation that the professional services have to be necessarily rendered to the person who makes payment to hospital. Therefore, TPAs who are making payment on behalf of insurance companies to hospitals for settlement of medical/insurance claims etc. under various schemes including cashless schemes are liable to deduct tax at source under section 194J on all such payments to hospitals etc.

In view of above, all such past transactions between TPAs and hospitals fall within provisions of section 194J and consequence of failure to deduct tax or after deducting tax failure to pay on all such transactions would make the deductor (TPAs) deemed to be an assessee in default in respect of such tax and also liable for charging of interest under section 201(1A) and penalty under section 271C.

Considering the facts and circumstances of the class of cases of TPAs and insurance companies, the Board has decided that no proceedings under section 201 may be initiated after the expiry of six years from the end of financial year in which such payment have been made without deducting tax at source etc. by the TPAs. The Board is also of the view that tax demand arising out of section 201(1) in situations arising above, may not be enforced if the deductor (TPA) satisfies the officer in charge of TDS that the relevant taxes have been paid by the deductee-assessee (hospitals etc.). A certificate from the auditor of the deductee-assessee stating that the tax and interest due from deductee-assessee has been paid for the assessment year concerned would be sufficient compliance for the above purpose. However, this will not alter the liability to charge interest under section 201(1A) till payment of taxes by the deductee-assessee or liability for penalty under section 271C, as the case may be - Circular : No. 8/2009, dated 24-11-2009. [Circular was partly set aside by the Bombay High Court in Dedicated Health Care Services TPA (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2010] 191 Taxman 1].
Exclusion from TDS under section 194J(1)(a) / TDS Not Applicable Cases:
Payments made for the acquisition of software:
Conditions when TDS Not Applicable:
The payment is for software acquired in a subsequent transfer without any modification.
Tax has been deducted under Section 194J on a previous transfer of the same software or under Section 195 on a previous transfer from a non-resident.
The transferee obtains a declaration from the transferor confirming that tax has been deducted, along with the transferor's Permanent Account Number (PAN).
Effective Date: This exemption is applicable from July 1, 2012.
Source: Notification No. 21/2012 [F.No.142/10/2012-SO(TPL)], dated 13-6-2012.

Annual maintenance contract - Payment towards AMC in respect of various specialised hospital equipments by assessee-hospital would not be in the nature of fees for technical services [CIT v. Asian Heart Institute & Research Centre (P.) Ltd. [2019] 104 taxmann.com 125/262 Taxman 395 (Bom.)].

Bill management service - Where assessee made payments towards bill management services, since said services were not in nature of professional services, rather it was a case of service contract, provisions of section 194J would not apply and, tax was required to be deducted u/s 194C in respect of said payments [CIT v. Executive Engineer [2015] 61 taxmann.com 414/234 Taxman 267 (Kar.), SLP granted in CIT v. Executive Engineer [2016] 69 taxmann.com 450/239 Taxman 511 (SC)].

Cable operators - Placement fees/carriage fees paid by assessee-company, engaged in business of distribution of television channels, to cable operators/MSO/DTH operators held not to be fees for technical service u/s 194J [CIT v. Times Global Broadcasting Co. Ltd. [2019] 105 taxmann.com 314/263 Taxman 465 (SC); CIT v. Zoom Entertainment Network Ltd. [2020] 117 taxmann.com 112/272 Taxman 101 (SC)].

Production related expenses by entertainment/ TV company The payment made by the entertainment/TV company to production house for programme software purchase, equipment hire charge and other production related expenses excluding dubbing and processing charges would be payments termed as fees for technical service under section 194J CIT v. Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 533/269 Taxman 569 (SC);

Contractual work- Where payee simply carried out a contractual work of up-linking and broadcasting programmes made or produced by assessee in electronic media by permitting assessee to avail benefit of requisite electronic set up against payment of fee as long as contract subsisted, facilities provided by payee did not amount to providing technical services [CIT v. Media World Wide (P.) Ltd. [2020] 120 taxmann.com 423/275 Taxman 272 (Cal.)].

Contract for supply - Where contract entered into by assessee with a consortium of companies in connection with contract for designing, manufacturing, supply, testing, commissioning of passenger rolling stock and training was an indivisible contract and dominant object of contract was supply of rolling stock and work taken up was ancillary to supply of rolling stock and did not amount to professional or technical service, payment made by assessee to consortium would not be liable to TDS u/s 194J [CIT v. Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Ltd. [2022] 140 taxmann.com 229/288 Taxman 539 (Kar.)].

Data collection charges - Data collection charges paid by assessee are not covered by the expression 'professional services' [CIT v. Market Probe India (P.) Ltd. [2014] 46 taxmann.com 166/227 Taxman 85 (Mag.) (Kar.)].

Doctors - Where contract with hospital and consultant doctors was one of contract for service and not contract of service, tax on payment to such doctors were to be deducted at source u/s 194J and section 192 had no application [CIT v. Apollo Hospitals International Ltd. [2014] 44 taxmann.com 368 (Guj.)]. Also see, CIT v. Asian Heart Institute & Research Centre (P.) Ltd. [2019] 104 taxmann.com 125/262 Taxman 395 (Bom.).

Payment made to retainer doctors for providing expertise professional services are subject to TDS to be deducted u/s 194J [Escorts Heart Institute & Research Centre Ltd. v. DCIT [2017] 87 taxmann.com 184/251 Taxman 401 (Raj.)].

Where assessee-company, engaged in business of running and operating a medical diagnostic centre, entered into contracts with doctors for providing medical diagnosis services in fields of radiology, pathology, cardiology, nuclear medicine etc. by using their personal knowledge, skills and expertise, amount paid to doctors for rendering said services was to be regarded as 'professional fee' requiring deduction of tax at source u/s 194J [CIT v. Teleradiology Solutions (P.) Ltd. [2016] 67 taxmann.com 346 (Kar.)].

Human intervention - Expression 'fees for technical services' as appearing in section 194J would have reference to only technical service rendered by a human; it would not include any service provided by machines or robots [CIT v. Bharti Cellular Ltd. [2008] 175 Taxman 573 (Delhi)]. If service rendered by a bank's MICR cheque processing centre involves human intervention requiring examination of technical data, same would fall within definition of 'technical service' [CIT v. Chief Manager, State Bank of India [2012] 21 taxmann.com 506 (P&H)].

Provisions of section 194J would have application only when the technology or technical knowledge of a person is made available to others and not where by using technical systems, services are rendered to others. Section 194J would apply where payment of fee for technical services would result in acquiring goods resulting in acquisition of certain rights which can be further used for assessee's own benefits/ use/purpose or research. ITO (TDS) v. Hindustan Zinc Ltd. [2013] 40 taxmann.com 42 (Jodh. - Trib.)
License fee - Licence fees paid to IRCTC is not in the nature of FTS [CIT v. Hakmichand D. & Sons [2017] 86 taxmann.com 21/250 Taxman 494 (Guj.)].

Mobile data utilisation - Payment made by assessee, a mobile service provider company, to another mobile service provider Company for utilization of roaming mobile data and connectivity could not be termed as technical service [CIT v. Vodafone South Ltd. [2016] 72 taxmann.com 347/241 Taxman 497 (Kar.), followed in CIT v. Tata Teleservices Ltd. [2022] 142 taxmann.com 51/288 Taxman 775 (Delhi)]. Services rendered by MTNL/other companies via interconnect/port access cannot be regarded as technical services as contemplated by section 194J [CIT v. Bharti Cellular Ltd. [2008] 175 Taxman 573 (Delhi)].

Reimbursement - No TDS liability on reimbursement of expenses incurred by C&F agent if separate bill was raised by him [PCIT v. Consumer Marketing (India) (P.) Ltd. [2015] 64 taxmann.com 16 (Guj.)]. Where under an arrangement entered into between assessee-bus stand management authority and State Road Transport Corporation, HRTC, assessee's work would initially be carried out by staff of HRTC till assessee developed its infrastructure, payment by assessee to HRTC could not be said to be made for rendering of professional services and, therefore, no TDS was to be deducted since it was only reimbursement of expenses [PCIT v. H. P. Bus Stand Management & Development Authority [2017] 86 taxmann.com 85/250 Taxman 496 (HP)].

Repair and maintenance - Where assessee made payments in respect of maintenance contracts which related to minor repairs, replacement of some spare parts, greasing of machinery etc., since, these services did not require any technical expertise, same could not be categorized as 'technical services' as contemplated u/s 194J [CIT v. Mumbai Metropolitan Regional Development Authority [2018] 97 taxmann.com 461/258 Taxman 164 (Bom.), SLP dismissed in CIT v. Mumbai Metropolitan Regional Development Authority [2019] 104 taxmann.com 210/262 Taxman 451 (SC)].

Revenue sharing - Sharing of revenue with franchisees through whom assessee was imparting computer education to Government employees and students could not be considered as payment of fees for professional or technical services [CIT v. Rajasthan Knowledge Corporation Ltd. [2017] 80 taxmann.com 237 (Raj.)].

Stock exchange service - Services made available by Bombay Stock Exchange [BSE Online Trading (BOLT) System] for which transaction charges are paid by members of BSE are common services that every member of Stock Exchange is necessarily required to avail of to carry out trading in securities in stock exchange; such services do not amount to 'technical services' provided by stock exchange, not being services specifically sought for by user or consumer and, therefore, no TDS would be deductible u/s 194J on payments made for such services [CIT v. Kotak Securities Ltd. [2016] 67 taxmann.com 356/239 Taxman 139 (SC)].

Subscription - Subscription payment made by assessee for financial e-magazine could not be considered as being in nature of any consultative/professional services rendered by that company to assessee [CIT v. India Capital Markets (P.) Ltd. [2017] 79 taxmann.com 45 (Bom.)].

Supply of data - Where parent company purchased a ready study data from a foreign company and supplied it to its subsidiary company (assessee) at cost, it could not be construed as technical services rendered to a resident u/s 194J [CIT v. Heramec Ltd. [2016] 68 taxmann.com 4/238 Taxman 519 (AP & Telangana); Asstt. CIT v. Gulbarga Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. [2016] 76 taxmann.com 244 (Kar.)].

Telephone services - When a person decides to subscribe to a cellular telephone service in order to have the facility of being able to communicate with others, he does not contract to receive a technical service. What he does agree is to pay for the use of the airtime for which he pays a charge. What applies to cellular mobile telephone is also applicable to fixed telephone service. Neither service can be regarded as 'technical service' for the purpose of section 194J [Skycell Communications Ltd. v. DCIT [2001] 119 Taxman 496/251 ITR 53 (Mad.)].

Third party administrators (TPAs) - TPA, who is responsible for making payment to hospitals for rendering medical services to policy holders under various health-insurance policies issued by several insurers, is obliged to deduct tax at source u/s 194J from payments made to hospitals [Medi Assist India TPA (P.) Applicability of TDS under section 194C
Provisions of this section are applicable when any payment is made to a contractor or subcontractor for carrying out any ‘work’ including supply of labour for carrying out any work.
As per explanation (iv) of section 194C Work shall include following:
advertising
broadcasting and telecasting including production of programmes for such broadcasting or telecasting.
carriage of goods or passengers by any mode of transport other than by railways
catering

manufacturing or supplying a product according to the requirement or specification of a customer by using material purchased from such customer or its associate, being a person related to the customer in such manner as defined u/s 40A(2)(b)

However, “work” shall not include manufacturing or supplying a product according to the requirement or specification of a customer by using raw material purchased from a person, other than such customer or associate of such customer, as such a contract is a contract for ‘sale’.
Rate of TDS
The applicable rates of TDS under section 194C are as follows:
The same rates of TDS would apply for both contractors and sub-contractors.
However, if the contractor fails to provide a valid PAN to the specified person, the tax shall be deducted at 20% according to section 206AA of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
In case the contractor is Non-Resident as per Income tax provisions, Rate of TDS shall be determined under different section i.e. under section 195.
Specified Threshold limit for deduction of tax at source under section 194C

Tax will be required to be deducted at source where the amount credited or paid or likely to be credited or paid to a contractor or sub-contractor exceeds Rs. 30,000 in a single payment or Rs.1,00,000 in the aggregate during a financial year.  Therefore, even if a single payment to a contractor does not exceed Rs.30,000, TDS provisions under section 194C would be attracted where the aggregate of the amounts of such sums credited or paid or likely to be credited or paid to the contractor during the financial year exceeds Rs. 1,00,000.
Person responsible for deducting tax at source under Section 194C:

Any “specified person” responsible for paying any sum to any resident contractor for carrying out any work (including supply of labor for carrying out any work) in pursuance of a contract shall be liable to deduct tax at source under section 194C.  The contract shall include any sub-contract.
As per explanation (i) of section 194C, specified persons shall mean:
the Central Government or any State Government; or
any local authority; or
any statutory corporation; or
any company; or
any co-operative society; or
any statutory authority dealing with housing accommodation; or
any society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860; or
any trust; or
any university established under a Central, State or Provincial Act and an institution declared to be a university under the UGC Act, 1956; or
any firm; or
any Government of a foreign State or foreign enterprise or any association or body established outside India; or

any person, being an individual, HUF, AOP or BOI, who has total sales, gross receipts or turnover from the business or profession carried on by him exceeding 1 crore in case of business and 50 lakhs in case of profession during the financial year immediately preceding the financial year in which such sum is credited or paid to the account of the contractor.

However, as per section 194C(4) an individual or HUF will not be liable to deduct tax on the sum credited or paid to the account of the resident contractor where such sum is credited or paid exclusively for personal purposes of such an individual or any member of HUF. However, in this case where TDS under section 194C is not applicable, TDS under section 194M may apply and hence the provision of section 194M needs to be checked.
Time of deduction
Tax has to be deducted at the time of payment of such sum or at the time of credit of such sum to the account of the contractor, whichever is earlier.

Where any such sum is credited to any account in the books of account of the person liable to pay such income, such crediting is deemed to be credit of such income to the account of the payee and the tax has to be deducted at source. The account to which such sum is credited may be called “Suspense account” or by any other name.
Exclusion when tax is not required to be deducted u/s 194C
In the following cases, tax is not required to be deducted at source:

When the sum paid or credited or likely to be paid or credited to the account of the resident contractor during the financial year exclusively for personal purposes of an individual or any member of Hindu undivided family.

When any sum paid or credited or likely to be paid or credited to the account of the resident contractor during the financial year does not exceed ₹30,000 in case of a single payment or ₹1,00,000 in case of aggregate payment.
In case, where payee applied in form 13 to AO for non-deduction, being his taxable income including rent below taxable limit, and has obtained certificate thereof.
As per Section 196 of Income tax act, 1961, no deduction of tax shall be made by any person from any sums payable to—
Government (i.e. State and Central Government)
RBI Corporation established under central act which is, under any law for the time being in force, exempt from income-tax on its income, or.
Mutual fund specified under section 10(23D).

Payment of Material – If any sum is required to be paid or credit for carrying out any work relating to manufacturing or supply of product as per the requirement or specification of a customer with the use of material supplied by such customer, tax shall be deducted:
On the invoice value excluding the value of material, if value of material is mentioned separately in the invoice
On the total value of invoice, if value of material is not mentioned separately in the invoice
Resident Transporter: If the following conditions are satisfied:
Amount is paid/credited to the account of any Resident Transporter who is engaged in the business of plying, hiring, or leasing of Goods Carriage vehicle;
Resident Transporter furnishes his Permanent Account Number (PAN) to the payer; and
He owns 10 or less than 10 Goods Carriage vehicles at any time during the financial year and furnishes a declaration to this effect to the payer.
Meaning of “Goods carriage”
As per income tax act "goods carriage" shall have the meaning shall be the meaning assigned in section 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
“Goods carriage” as per motor vehicle act means –
any motor vehicle constructed or adapted for use solely for the carriage of goods; or
any motor vehicle not so constructed or adapted, when used for the carriage of goods.

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 has amended 194C to provide that any sum referred to in Section 194J(1) does not constitute "work" for the purposes of TDS under Section 194C. The CBDT has earlier clarified that the provisions of Section 194C do not apply if a specific type of work falls under the TDS provisions of Section 194J. The need for this clarification arose due to the differing TDS rates stipulated in these sections. Under Section 194C, the TDS rate is either 1% or 2%, whereas under Section 194J, the rate is generally 10%, except for payments for technical services, which are subject to a 2% TDS rate. Therefore, if a payment falls under both Sections 194C and 194J, the assessee does not have the discretion to choose the TDS section. TDS must be deducted under Section 194J.
Important points
The deduction of income-tax at source from payments made to non-resident contractors will be governed by the provisions of section 195.

The deduction of income-tax will be made from sums paid for carrying out any work or for supplying labour for carrying out any work. In other words, the section will apply only in relation to ‘works contracts’ and ‘labour contracts’ and will not cover contracts for sale of goods.

Contracts for rendering professional services by lawyers, physicians, surgeons, engineers, accountants, architects, consultants etc., cannot be regarded as contracts for carrying out any “work” and, accordingly, no deduction of income-tax is to be made from payments relating to such contracts under this section. Separate provisions for fees for professional services have been made under section 194J.
