Illustrative transactions:

Payments to munshis in bidi industry - In the bidi manufacturing industry, the provisions of section 194C would apply in respect of payments made to munshis. By the very nature of the functions performed by the munshis, there is an implied contract between the manufacturer and the munshis and consequently the munshis are contractors even though there is no written contract or agreement.—Circular : No. 433, dated 25-9-1985. The deductions under section 194C to be made from the payments to munshis need not include payments to such home workers as are employed through the medium of agency such as munshis but the workers bring bidi to the factory for quality check and for getting their payments.—Circular : No. 487, dated 8-6-1987.

Works executed under NREP and RLEGP - The provisions of section 194C are not attracted in the case of payments made in respect of works executed under the National Rural Employment Programme (NREP) and Rural Landless Employment Guarantee Programme (RLEGP)—Circular: No. 502, dated 27-1-1988.

Payments to RTCs - Section 194C can be applied qua payments made by a State Road Transport Corporation to private bus owners, from whom buses are hired for plying on specified routes.—Circular : No. 558, dated 28-3-1990.

Hiring or renting of equipment – The provisions of section 194C would not apply in relation to payments made for hiring or renting of equipments, etc. Case reference - Associated Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1993] 201 ITR 435. Circular : No. 681, dated 8-3-1994.

Transactions in negotiable instruments: The provisions of section 194C would not apply in relation to payments made to banks for discounting bills collecting/receiving payments through cheques/drafts, opening and negotiating Letters of Credit and transactions in negotiable instruments. Case law referred - Associated Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1993] 201 ITR 435. Circular : No. 681, dated 8-3-1994.

Contracts - The provisions of section 194C shall apply to all types of contracts for carrying out any work including, transport contracts, service contracts, advertisement contracts, broadcasting contracts, telecasting contracts, labour contracts, material contracts and works contracts. Case law referred - Associated Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1993] 201 ITR 435. Circular : No. 681, dated 8-3-1994.

Contract for fabrication of articles or things as per specification given by assessee - Representations have been received in the Board seeking clarification on the applicability of section 194C on such transactions, where the assessee has outsourced certain work relating to fabrication or manufacturing of article or thing in accordance with the specifications given by the assessee. Circular No. 681, dated 8-3-1994 of the Board clarifies in para 7(vi) that the provisions of section 194C would not apply to contracts for sale of goods and further clarifies that where the property in the article or thing so fabricated passes from the fabricator-contractor to the assessee only after such article or thing is delivered to the assessee, such contract would be a contract for sale and so outside the purview of section 194C. However, in reply to question No. 15 in Circular No. 715, dated 8-8-1995 on the subject of applicability of section 194C, in respect of contract for supply of printed material as per prescribed specifications, it has been said that such contracts would also be covered under section 194C. It has been represented that the views expressed in these two circulars, to the extent as pointed out above, are in contradiction to each other.

The matter has been examined by the Board and it is considered that exclusive reliance on Question/Answer No. 15 of Circular No. 715, without taking into account the principles laid down in Circular No. 681 is not justified. Before taking a decision on the applicability of TDS under section 194C on a contract, it would have to be examined whether the contract in question is a 'contract for work' or a 'contract for sale' and TDS shall be applicable only where it is a 'contract for work'.

It is, therefore, clarified that the provisions of section 194C would apply in respect of a contract for supply of any article or thing as per prescribed specifications only if it is a contract for work and not a contract for sale as per the principles in this regard laid down in para 7(vi) of Circular No. 681, dated 8-3-1994—Circular : No. 13/2006, dated 13-12-2006.
Works contract -

Where contract between assessee and HTMT/HGSL was in nature of a 'works contract' and not of technical or professional nature, payments made by assessee to these entities towards call centre expenses would be covered u/s 194C and not u/s 194J [PCIT v. National Health & Education Society [2019] 103 taxmann.com 286/262 Taxman 240 (Bom.)].

Where assessee-transporter had given sub-contracts to dumper owners for transportation of goods and dumpers were not taken on hire/rent, payments to sub-contractors would attract provisions of section 194C since contract for shifting of goods from one place to another would be covered as works contract [CIT v. Shree Mahalaxmi Transport Co. [2012] 19 taxmann.com 144/211 Taxman 232 (Guj.)].

Subcontracting Fabrication Work- For the subcontracting of fabrication work where Assessee supplies material and specifications to the vendor, the contract is considered a work contract under Section 194C. The tax withholding obligation applies to the payments made to the vendor for the service charges, excluding the cost of materials supplied by Assessee, provided the cost is separately mentioned in the invoice.

Payments to airlines/travel agents - The provisions of section 194C do not apply to the payments made to the airlines or the travel agents for purchase of tickets for air travel of individuals. The provisions shall however apply when payments are made for chartering an aircraft for carriage of passengers or goods. This clarification will apply mutatis mutandis to the tickets for travel of individual by any other mode of transport also—Circular : No. 713, dated 2-8-1995.

The payments made to a travel agent or an airline for purchase of a ticket for travel would not be subjected to tax deduction at source as the privity of the contract is between the individual passenger and the airline/travel agent, notwithstanding the fact that the payment is made by an entity mentioned in section 194C(1). The provisions of section 194C shall however apply when a plane or a bus or any other mode of transport is chartered by one of the entities mentioned in section 194C—Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.

Airport charges that are paid by international airlines to AAI for landing and take-off services as well as for parking of aircrafts are not, in substance, for use of land but for various other facilities extended by AAI in connection with aircraft operation and, hence, such charges are covered u/s 194C [Japan Airlines Co. Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 60 taxmann.com 71/234 Taxman 175 (SC), affirming CIT v. Singapore Airlines Ltd. [2012] 24 taxmann.com 200/209 Taxman 581 (Mad.)].

Advertisement contract- Regarding the scope and meaning of the term 'advertising' used in section 194C(1), it is clarified that advertising may be in print or electronic media, i.e., in newspapers, periodicals, radio, television, etc. In such cases, tax will be deducted at the rate of 1 per cent of the payment made for advertising including production of programmes for such broadcasting and telecasting to be used in such advertising. In all other cases of work of broadcasting and telecasting including production of programmes for such broadcasting and telecasting, where advertising is not involved, tax will be deducted at the rate of 2 per cent of the sum—Circular : No. 714, dated 3-8-1995.
Clarifications on advertising contracts - The following clarifications need be noted:

As to the scope of an advertising contract for the purpose of section 194C, the term 'advertising' has not been defined in the Act. During the course of consideration of the Finance Bill, 1995, the Finance Minister clarified on the floor of the House that the amended provisions of tax deduction at source would apply when a client makes payment to an advertising agency and not when advertising agency makes payment to the media, which includes both print and electronic media. The deduction is required to be made at the rate of 1 per cent. When an advertising agency makes payments to their models, artists, photographers, etc., the tax shall be deducted at the rate of 5 per cent as applicable to fees for professional and technical services under section 194J of the Act.

If the advertising agencies give a consolidated bill including charges for art work and other related jobs as well as payments made by them to media, the deduction will have to be made under section 194C at the rate of 1 per cent. The advertising agencies shall have to deduct tax at source at the rate of 5 per cent under section 194J while making payments to artists, actors, models, etc. If payments are made for production of programmes for the purpose of broadcasting and telecasting, these payments will be subject to TDS at 2 per cent. Even if the production of such programmes is for the purpose of preparing advertisement material, not for immediate advertising, the payment will be subject to TDS at the rate of 2 per cent.

The payments made directly to print and electronic media would be covered under section 194C as these are in the nature of payments for purpose of advertising. Deduction will have to be made at the rate of 1 per cent. However, the payments made directly to Doordarshan may not be subjected to TDS as Doordarshan, being a Government agency, is not liable to income-tax.

The contract for putting up a hoarding is in the nature of advertising contract and provisions of section 	 would be applicable. However, if a person has taken a particular space on rent and thereafter sublets the same fully or in part for putting up a hoarding, he would be liable to TDS under section 194-I and not under section 194C. In the case of advertising contracts, tax is to be deducted at the rate of 1 per cent of the gross amount of the bill (including bill of media), and not on that portion of commission paid to the person who arranges release of advertisement, etc.

In the case of sponsorship for debates, seminars and other functions held in colleges, schools and associations with a view to earn publicity through display of banners, etc., put up by the organisers, the agreement of sponsorship is in essence an agreement for carrying out a work of advertisement. Therefore, provisions of section 194C will apply.
Tax is deductible at source on payments for costs of advertisements issued in the souvenirs brought out by various organisations—Circular No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.
Case reference :

Where assessee-company purchased an advertisement space in a local newspaper and exercised control over such space with right to either sell it to other or retain it for itself, payment made by assessee for purchase of such advertisement space would not be liable for tax deduction at source u/s 194C [Times VPL Ltd. v. CIT [2020] 120 taxmann.com 356/275 Taxman 176 (Kar.)].

Sub-agents of advertising agencies receiving payments from clients are not supposed to deduct TDS u/s 194C while remitting same to advertising agencies [CIT v. Honest Publicity [2013] 38 taxmann.com 198/219 Taxman 272 (Guj.)].

Payment for Advertising Services - Payments made by an advertising agency to media companies, including radio media, for advertisement placement are not subject to TDS under Section 194C. This is supported by CBDT Circular No. 715 and Circular No. 5/2016, which clarify that while TDS applies to payments made by clients to advertising agencies, it does not apply to payments made by ad agencies to media companies.

Cost of Procuring Media Space and Media Agency Commission- withholding tax implications on the cost of procuring media space and media agency commission. Entire payment made for procuring media space would be covered under Section 194C. Alternatively, if the recipient acts as an agent of the payer, Section 194C will apply to the reimbursement portion (for procuring media space) and Section 194H would apply to the commission amount. The relationship between the payer and the media agency can be viewed as an agency relationship, thus commissions paid to the agent would attract Section 194H. The reimbursement for media cost should be considered under Section 194C while the commission should be considered under Section 194H. In the absence of specific judicial precedents, assessee should cautiously apply Section 194C to avoid potential interest, penalty, and disallowance of expenses.

Broadcasters or television channels to production houses for production of content or programme for telecasting - The issue of applicability of TDS provisions on payments made by broadcasters/telecasters to production houses for production of content or programme for broadcasting/telecasting has been examined by CBDT in view of representations received in this regard.

2. It has been noted that disputes have arisen on the issue as to whether payments made by the broadcaster/telecaster to production houses for production of content/programme are payments under a 'work contract' or a contract for 'professional or technical services' and, therefore, liable for TDS u/s 194C or u/s 194J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act').

3. While applying the relevant provision of TDS on a contract for content production, a distinction is required to be made between (i) a payment for production of content/programme as per the specifications of the broadcaster/telecaster and (ii) a payment for acquisition of broadcasting/telecasting rights of the content already produced by the production house.

4. In the first situation where the content is produced as per the specifications provided by the broadcaster/telecaster and the copyright of the content/programme also gets transferred to the telecaster/broadcaster, it is hereby clarified that such contract is covered by the definition of the term 'work' in section 194C of the Act and, therefore, subject to TDS under that section. This position clearly flows from the definition of 'work' given in clause (iv)(b) of the Explanation to section 194C and the same has also been clarified vide Qn. No. 3 of Circular No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.

5. However, in a case where the telecaster/broadcaster acquires only the telecasting/broadcasting rights of the content already produced by the production house, there is no contract for 'carrying out any work', as required in sub-section (1) of section 194C. Therefore, such payments are not liable for TDS under section 194C. However, payments of this nature may be liable for TDS under other sections under Chapter XVII-C of the Act.—Circular No. 4/2016, dated 29-2-2016.

Warehousing charges - Tax is deductible u/s 194C in relation to warehousing charges paid to clearing and forwarding agents [CIT v. Hindustan Lever Ltd. [2013] 29 taxmann.com 313/ 216 Taxman 280 (Delhi)].

Clearing and forwarding agents - Payments made to clearing and forwarding agents for carriage of goods are subjected to deduction of tax at source under section 194C, since unlike the travel agents, they are independent contractors. They would also be liable to deduct tax at source while making payments to a carrier of goods—Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.

Handling charges - Where assessee was engaged in business of clearing and forwarding of cargo, etc., and it made payments towards cargo handling charges to two parties and work involved was mainly labour oriented work with help of various machineries and equipments, TDS provisions of section 194C would be applicable with respect to said payments [CIT v. Aditya Marine Ltd. [2014] 41 taxmann.com 381/224 Taxman 169 (Guj.)].
Payments to transporters –

In the case of payments to transporters, each GR can be said to be a separate contract, if the goods are transported at one time. But if the goods are transported continuously in pursuance of a contract for a specific period or quantity, each GR will not be a separate contract and all GRs relating to that period or quantity will be aggregated for the purpose of TDS. Even when the goods are received on 'freight to pay' basis, the TDS provisions would be applicable, irrespective of the actual payment—Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.

The assessee had given sub-contracts for transportation of goods. Therefore, the transactions would fall within the purview of section 194C as the assessee was responsible for paying the amount in question for carrying out work in pursuance of contracts between the assessee and the transporters and as such the assessee was required to deduct tax at source at the rate prescribed under that section [CIT V. Swayam Shipping Services P. Ltd., (2011) 339 ITR 647 (Guj)]

Owning and operating - Where members of assessee-association were engaged in business of owning and operating vessels for which they entered into contracts of transport service in form of charter parties, tax from freight payments had to be deducted under section 194C and not under section 194-I. (Indian National Ship Owners Association v. Commissioner of Income-tax, [2023] 154 taxmann.com 294 (Bombay)

Payments to couriers - The carriage of documents, letters, etc., is in the nature of carriage of goods, and therefore, provisions of section 194C would be attracted in respect of payments made to the couriers—Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.

Commission agent - Where assessee carried on business of commission agent by arranging for transportation of goods through other transporters, in view of the fact that assessee only acted as intermediary and, there was no privity of contract between assessee and clients, assessee was not liable to deduct tax at source while making payments to transporters [CIT v. Hardarshan Singh [2013] 30 taxmann.com 245/216 Taxman 283 (Delhi)].

Payments to restaurants/cafes - TDS is not required to be made when payment is made for serving food in a restaurant in the normal course of running of the restaurant/cafe—Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.

Payments to recruitment agencies - Payments to recruitment agencies are in the nature of payments for services rendered and not for carrying out any work including supply of labour for carrying out any work. Hence provisions of section 194C will not apply. The payments will however be subjected to TDS under section 194J. Similar would be the position in respect of payments made by a company to a share registrar—Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.
FD commission/brokerage - FD commission and brokerage are not covered under section 194C—Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.
Supply of printed material - Supply of printed material is covered by section 194C—Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.

Rendering of services by external parties - Rendering of services by external parties for procurement of orders is not covered under section 194C. If rendering of such services involved payment of fees for professional or technical services, tax may be deductible under section 194J—Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.

Electrical contracts - Where the services of a regular electrician are engaged on a contract basis or the services of an electrician are provided by a contractor, the payments made to the electrician or the contractor will be in the nature of payment made in pursuance of a contract for carrying out any work, and provisions of section 194C will apply in such cases—Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.
Maintenance contracts –

Routine maintenance contracts including supply of spares would be covered under section 194C. However, where technical services are rendered, the provisions of section 194J will apply in regard to tax deduction at source—Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.

Where assessee had a contract for repairing of transformers, tax u/s 194C was rightly deducted only on labour charges by excluding value of material used by contractor for repairing of transformers [CIT v. Executive Engineer (Electricity Stores), Distribution Division [2013] 35 taxmann.com 614/217 Taxman 199 (Mag.) (All.)].

Payment towards annual maintenance contract (AMC) in respect of various specialised hospital equipments by assessee-hospital would fall u/s 194C as payment to contractor [CIT v. Asian Heart Institute & Research Centre (P.) Ltd. [2019] 104 taxmann.com 125/262 Taxman 395 (Bom.)].

Where assessee-company paid certain amount as common area maintenance (CAM) charges, provision of section 194C was applicable on said payment; provision of section 194-I was not attracted. [Welgrow Hotels Concepts (P.) Ltd. v. Income-tax Officer, [2023] 156 taxmann.com 144 (Delhi - Trib.)]

Reimbursement of expenses – Where gross amount of the bill includes reimbursements of actual expenses, Section 194C is applicable as it refers to 'any sum paid'. Thus reimbursement of actual expenses cannot be deducted out of the bill amount for the purpose of tax deduction at source—Circular : No. 715, dated 8-8-1995.
Case in Favour of TDS applicable:

Deduction of tax at source under section 194C is required to be made on any sum paid by assessee engaged in business of generation and distribution of power to clearing and forwarding agent and it includes reimbursement of expenditure, in Surendra Commercial & Exim (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2022] 141 taxmann.com 23/288 Taxman 580 (Cal.) , Further, (Special leave petition) SLP dismissed in Surendra Commercial & Exim (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2022] 145 taxmann.com 639 (SC), it has been held that since assessee had failed to produce any document in support to its contention, it was liable to deduct tax at source even in respect of reimbursements which had been incurred by agent.
Case in Favour of TDS Not applicable:

While reimbursing clearing and forwarding agents amount of freight charges paid by them on behalf of assessee, no TDS liability would arise [CIT v. Opera Global (P.) Ltd. [2014] 52 taxmann.com 299 (Delhi); Sima Agencies v. ITO [2021] 126 taxmann.com 109/279 Taxman 171 (Mad.); Zephyr Biomedicals v. JCIT [2020] 122 taxmann.com 124/[2021] 276 Taxman 305 (Bom.)].

Where seller sold goods to assessee (buyer) and under contract of sale, it was bound to send goods to buyer and to pay transportation charges to goods transport agency and assessee reimbursed freight component to seller and claimed deduction of same, assessee was not liable to deduct tax at source u/s 194C in respect of freight component [Hightension Switchgears (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2016] 71 taxmann.com 207/240 Taxman 582 (Cal.)].

Reimbursement to Employee for Catering Services – The privity of the contract was between the employer (company) and the caterer. The employee acted as a disbursing agent on behalf of the company. The transaction is covered under Section 194C, thus tax withholding under Section 194C is attracted. The reimbursement to the employee should not involve any tax withholding in the hands of employee as it is a cost-only basis repayment.

Outsourcing arrangement qualifies as a "contract of work" or a "contract of sale" depends on factors such as the transfer of property, the source of raw material, and the dominant interest and object of the contract. If materials supplied by the purchaser are incidental and the supplier procures major components from third parties, it may qualify as a sale contract. Conversely, if the purchaser's materials are significant, it qualifies as a works contract under Section 194C.

Applicability to shipping business of non-residents - It is clear from section 194C that the area of operation of TDS is confined to payments made to any 'resident'. On the other hand, section 172 operates in the area of computation of profits from shipping business of non-residents. Thus, there is no overlapping in the areas of operation of these sections. Since the provisions of section 172 override other provisions of the Act, the provisions of section 194C are not applicable to non-resident shipping business. Even where payments are made to shipping agents of non-resident ship-owners or charterers for carriage of passengers, etc., shipped at a port in India, the agent acts on behalf of the non-resident ship-owner or charterers and thus steps into the shoes of the principal. Hence, even in such cases, section 194C will not apply—Circular: No. 723, dated 19-9-1995.

Gas transportation charges by the purchaser of natural gas to the seller of gas - The main stakeholders in Oil & Gas Industry are the - owners/sellers of the gas (which could be a Gas Distribution Company); Transporters of gas (which could be the Owners/Sellers of the gas or a third party/parties) and the purchasers/end-users of the gas. The Owner/Seller of the gas may transfer the ownership of the gas to the purchaser either at the point of delivery at the premises of the purchaser or at any intermediate point.

It is clarified that in case the Owner/Seller of the gas sells as well as transports the gas to the purchaser till the point of delivery, where the ownership of gas to the purchaser is simultaneously transferred, the manner of raising the sale bill (whether the transportation charges are embedded in the cost of gas or shown separately) does not alter the basic nature of such contract which remains essentially a 'contract for sale' and not a 'works contract' as envisaged in section 194C of the Act. Hence in such circumstances, provisions of Chapter XVII-B of the Act are not applicable on the component of Gas Transportation Charges paid by the purchaser to the Owner/Seller of the gas. The use of different modes of transportation of gas by Owner/Seller will not alter the position. It is needless to mention that transportation charges paid to a third party transporter of gas, either by the Owner/Seller of the gas or purchaser of the gas or any other person, shall continue to be governed by the appropriate provisions of the Act and TDS shall be deductible on such payment to the third party at the applicable rates - Circular No. 9/2012, dated 17-10-2012.

Professional contractors are to be excluded - The word 'contractor' in section 194C, as used in the context of that provision, refers to businessmen who do contract work, and not professionals like lawyers, chartered accountants, doctors, engineers, etc. Thus, Circular No. 681, dated 8-3-1994, which makes section 194C applicable to professionals is to be quashed [Moradabad Chartered Accountants Association v. CBDT [2004] 137 Taxman 496 (All.)].
Sub-contractor -

A 'sub-contractor' would mean any person who enters into a contract with the contractor for carrying out or for the supply of labour for carrying out the whole or part of the work undertaken by the contractor under a contract or for the supply whether wholly or partly any labour which the contractor has undertaken to supply in terms of his contract [ITO v. Rama Nand & Co. [1987] 30 Taxman 434 (HP)].
The truck operators if not the truck owners, cannot be considered as the sub-contractors for the purpose of section 194C(2) [Shivamurthy v. Addl. CIT [2022] 140 taxmann.com 331 (Kar.)].

Disallowance irrespective of method of accounting followed - Requirement to deduct TDS u/s 194C is mandatory and, in case of assessee's failure to do so in respect of contractual payments, disallowance has to be made u/s 40(a)(ia) irrespective of fact as to whether assessee is following cash or mercantile system of accounting [P. M. S. Diesels v. CIT [2015] 59 taxmann.com 100/232 Taxman 544 (P&H)].

Oral contract - Where assessee made payments on regular basis to owners of goods carrying vehicles though in terms of oral contract, assessee was liable to deduct TDS u/s 194C [CIT v. Md. Tabarak [2015] 61 taxmann.com 94/234 Taxman 115 (Jharkhand)].

Where assessee-hospital engaged two ladies to facilitate and manage its drug store, drug handling charges paid to said ladies would be liable to deduction of tax at source u/s 194C [CIT v. Jaslok Hospital & Research Centre [2015] 59 taxmann.com 145/232 Taxman 538 (Bom.)].

TDS deduction on sum credited, not on income component - Amount of TDS required to be deducted by payer out of sum credited to account of or paid to contractor is not to be confined to his income component out of that sum, but it has to be deducted on sum credited to account of or paid to contractor in pursuance of contract [Associated Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1993] 67 Taxman 346 (SC)].

Bill management service - Where assessee made payments towards bill management services, since said services were not in nature of professional services, rather it was a case of service contract, provisions of section 194J would not apply and, tax was required to be deducted u/s 194C in respect of said payments [CIT v. Executive Engineer [2015] 61 taxmann.com 414/234 Taxman 267 (Kar.), SLP granted in CIT v. Executive Engineer [2016] 69 taxmann.com 450/239 Taxman 511 (SC)].

Payments for Cash Management Services - Payments for services like cash collection and remittance are not covered under Section 194C. The service is seen as a banking or insurance service, and thus, no withholding obligation arises under Section 194C.

Cable operators - Placement fees/carriage fees paid by assessee to cable operators, MSO/DTH operators would be covered u/s 194C [CIT v. Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd. [2018] 92 taxmann.com 30/254 Taxman 370 (Bom.), SLP dismissed in CIT v. Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd. [2020] 117 taxmann.com 132/272 Taxman 116 (SC); CIT v. Times Global Broadcasting Co. Ltd. [2019] 105 taxmann.com 314/263 Taxman 465 (SC); CIT v. Disney Broadcasting (India) Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 249/269 Taxman 464 (SC)].

Where assessee-company, carrying on business of broadcasting of television channels, made payment of subtitling charges for writing dialogues in a particular language other than language of film or TV programme, it being a 'work' and, thus, assessee was justified in deducting tax at source u/s 194C while making said payments [CIT v. Disney Broadcasting (India) Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 249/269 Taxman 464 (SC)].

Where payee simply carried out a contractual work of up-linking and broadcasting programmes made or produced by assessee in electronic media by permitting assessee to avail benefit of requisite electronic set up against payment of fee as long as contract subsisted, facilities provided by payee did not amount to providing technical services and, hence, payments could not be termed as fees for technical services u/s 194J and would be liable to TDS u/s 194C [CIT v. Media World Wide (P.) Ltd. [2020] 120 taxmann.com 423/275 Taxman 272 (Cal.)].

Carriage fees paid to cable operators for transmitting TV channels will fall under Section 194C or 194J. In this case the nature of payment was more in the nature of a service contract rather than "carrying out any work" and thus does not fall under Section 194C.

Octroi collection - Where the assessee was awarded a contract by a municipal committee for collection of octroi, tax is deductible at source on the amount paid to the assessee by the municipal committee, and not on the amount of octroi collected by the assessee [S. S. & Co., Octroi Contractors v. State of Punjab [2004] 268 ITR 398 (P&H)].

Sub-contractors- Where assessee had entered into a contract with a cement company to transport cement and for that assessee hired services of truck owners as sub-contractors, assessee would be liable to deduct tax at source u/s 194C from payments made to truck owners [Shree Choudhary Transport Company v. ITO [2020] 118 taxmann.com 47/272 Taxman 472 (SC)].

Hire charges - Where assessee took certain vehicles on hire for carrying its students and staff, it was justified in deducting tax at source u/s 194C while making payments of hiring charges to transport contractor [Asstt. CIT v. Lotus Valley Education Society [2014] 45 taxmann.com 37/223 Taxman 82 (Mag.) (All.)]. However, where assessee, in pursuance of contract of transporting employees of an institute, hired vehicles from a private agency, in view of the fact that assessee had only rented vehicles and said agency had not provided any service of carriage of passengers, assessee was not required to deduct tax at source u/s 194C while making payment of hiring charges [CIT v. Mukesh Travels Co. [2014] 43 taxmann.com 47/224 Taxman 174 (Guj.)].

Cab Hire Arrangement- In the proposed arrangement, the employee directly engages with Cab rental Vendor, and Assesee Company merely facilitates the arrangement by providing Amex corporate cards. The privity of contract is between the employee and Cab rental vendor, and hence, Section 194C is not applicable to the cab hire charges. However, as a conservative approach to avoid litigation, it is suggested to either withhold tax or obtain a Section 197 certificate.

Hiring of vehicles- Hiring of vehicles does not fall within ambit of section 194C and w.e.f. 1-6-2007 TDS for hiring of vehicles is to be deducted u/s 194-I [CIT v. Pioneer Peresonalised Holidays (P.) Ltd. [2018] 92 taxmann.com 107 (Ker.)].
Taxi-owners –

Assessee-company, engaged in business of operation of tourist taxis, was liable to deduct tax. Assessee hired taxis from various owners to operate its business. Payments made to these taxi owners are considered payments to contractors. [CIT v. Janani Tours & Resorts (P.) Ltd. [2015] 63 taxmann.com 347 (Kar.)].
Payments made by the cab owner to the driver under the revenue-sharing model do not constitute "work" but are for services rendered, thus not attracting Section 194C.

Aggregator to taxi operators: withholding tax implications on various payments made by an aggregator to taxi operators, such as trip subsidies, guaranteed revenue, performance incentives, and referral bonuses. Trip subsidies and guaranteed revenue payments fall under Section 194C due to their connection with the carriage of passengers. Performance incentives also fall under Section 194C. However, referral bonuses do not fall under Section 194C or Section 194H as they do not involve an agency relationship or the carriage of goods
Single integrated agreement -

Where three different contracts entered into by assessee with its sister concern were found to be in nature of a single integrated agreement for construction of refinery plant which could be termed as 'works contract', assessee was required to deduct tax at source u/s 194C while making payments to its sister concern [Essar Oil Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 30 taxmann.com 39/215 Taxman 365 (Guj.)].

Contracts entered into by assessee-company with various contractors to execute work of erection, testing, commissioning and trial operation of power cycle piping, boiler and LP piping packages for various units in State, amounted to works contract requiring deduction of tax at source u/s 194C [PCIT v. Senior Manager (Finance), Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. [2017] 77 taxmann.com 269 (P&H)].
Composite nature of contract-

Where assessee entered into indivisible contracts with BHEL and CIPL for setting up of thermal power plant, since element of testing and commissioning of technical works etc. were part of main contract, in absence of any internal tool arising from contract or in absence of any legal provision allowing AO to break down indivisibility or composite nature of contract, dominant object of contract could not be overlooked, to conclude existence of component of FTS and thus, TDS with respect to payment made by assessee was to be made under section 194C [HIGH COURT OF ALLAHABAD- Commissioner of Income-tax (TDS) v. Lalitpur Power Generation Co. Ltd, [2023] 156 taxmann.com 698 (Allahabad)]

In a case where three separate agreements were entered into, i.e., one for supply of goods, second for erection works and third for civil engineering work, section 194C cannot be pressed into service to deduct tax at source on payment for supply of material merely because said agreement is a part of composite transaction [CIT v. Karnataka Power Transmission Corporation Ltd. [2012] 21 taxmann.com 473/208 Taxman 73 (Kar.)].

Comprehensive contracts: Contracts for civil works and comprehensive contracts involving engineering and erection are generally covered under Section 194C. Routine maintenance services also fall under Section 194C, whereas involved technical services might fall under Section 194J.

Processing of milk- Assessee made payments to a dairy for conversion of raw milk into processed milk and milk products and deducted tax at source under section 194C at rate of 2 per cent - Assessing Officer held that payments were in nature of payments for technical services and same should have been subjected to TDS at rate of 10 per cent under section 194J- Tribunal held that processing of milk would fall under section 194C. [Principal Commissioner of Income-tax v. Maahi Milk Producer Co. Ltd., [2023] 156 taxmann.com 217 (Gujarat)]

Customised products - Where tenderer supplied sachets to assessee-milk producer society as per its specifications by securing material from external source, it could not be held as works contract [CIT v. Bangalore District Co-operative Milk Producers Societies Union Ltd. [2013] 36 taxmann.com 120/[2014] 220 Taxman 398 (Kar.)].

Payment for Supply of Milk: The supply of milk by vendors procured from milk suppliers and sold to vendors should not be covered by the term 'work' under Section 194C, considering the exclusion provided in the section. The transaction is seen as a principal-to-principal basis, and thus, the provisions of Section 194C do not apply.

No contract  - In the absence of any contract entered by assessee with a specific person to get any work done by such person, provisions of section 194C would not be attracted and assessee would have no liability to deduct TDS [PCIT v. Swastik Construction [2018] 91 taxmann.com 10/254 Taxman 163 (Guj.)].

No sub-contract - Where assessee-union was formed by truck operators in order to obtain bigger contracts through it and freight received from parties was disbursed to concerned truck operators, there being no sub-contract between assessee and its members, assessee was not liable to deduct tax out of freight belonging and disbursed to members. Thus, where relationship between assessee and transporter was not that of contractor and sub-contractor, section 194C held not attracted [CIT v. Truck Operators' Union [2012] 20 taxmann.com 848 (P&H); CIT v. Prashant H Shah [2013] 29 taxmann.com 296/216 Taxman 287 (Guj.)].

Contract for sale/purchase - Where assessee entered into a contract with GAIL for supply of gas to its consumption points through pipelines and in addition to price of gas it had agreed to make separate payments for transportation of gas, contract was a contract for purchase of gas and not a work contract [CIT v. Krishak Bharati Co-operative Ltd. [2012] 27 taxmann.com 304/211 Taxman 236 (Guj.)]. Also see, CIT v. Krishna Kumar Goel [2014] 41 taxmann.com 113/224 Taxman 165 (All.); CIT v. Khadim Shoes (P.) Ltd. [2015] 61 taxmann.com 413/234 Taxman 297 (Cal.).

Sale transaction - Where assessee, a sugar manufacturer, made payments to transporters, it has been held that since supply of sugarcane by farmers at gate of factory of assessee was a part of sale transaction, therefore, assessee was not liable to deduct tax at source [Asstt. CIT v. Khedut Sahakari Khand Udyog Mandi Ltd. [2016] 76 taxmann.com 137/243 Taxman 522 (SC)].

Sale of area - Where assessee had entered into agreements with owners of land for construction of complex and it was to be allotted some area in complex with full liberty to sell, transfer and convey said area in favour of third party and it had assigned its rights in favour of one 'P', it was a case of sale of area in complex and it could not be said that assessee had engaged 'P' as its contractor, and therefore section 194C was not attracted in subject case [Asstt. CIT v. Alfran Construction (P.) Ltd. [2020] 116 taxmann.com 125 (Bom.)].

Payment to employees - Where payments were made to employees employed by assessee on daily wages, such payments could not be said to be contractual payments so as to attract TDS u/s 194C [CIT v. Dewan Chand [2009] 178 Taxman 173 (Delhi)].

When payment not made by intermediary contractor - Assessee received transportation charges as contractor of various companies and then made payment to various persons/truck owners for carrying out work as sub-contractor. AO found that assessee did not deduct tax on payments made for carrying out work of one company. The High Court held that section 194C r/w section 204(iii) will come into operation only on payment made by assessee. There was an agreement between said company and assessee that freight payment would be made by said company directly to truck owners and TDS deduction as applicable would be made by said company; since payment was not made by assessee, default in TDS was that of other company and not assessee [CIT v. Daulat Enterprises [2018] 94 taxmann.com 262/256 Taxman 211 (SC)].
Movie distribution - Cine-casting/distribution of movies would be outside the purview of section 194C [CIT v. City Gold Entertainment (P.) Ltd. [2015] 54 taxmann.com 256/229 Taxman 215 (Guj.)].

Ancillary services provided by hotels - The services rendered by a hotel to its customers by making available certain facilities/amenities like providing multi-lingual staff, 24-hour service for reception, telephones, selected restaurants, bank counter, beauty saloon, barber shop, car rental, shopping centre, laundry/valet, health club, business centre services, etc., do not involve carrying out any work which results in production of the desired object and, therefore, would be outside the purview of section 194C [East India Hotels Ltd. v. CBDT [2009] 179 Taxman 17 (Bom.)].
Electricity distribution companies –

Where assessee, engaged in distribution of electricity, made payments of wheeling charges, power factor rebate, unscheduled interchanging charges, transmission charges, power interruption charges, said payments not being in nature of contractual payments nor were they for receiving technical services, assessee was not required to deduct tax at source u/s 194C or 194J [PCIT v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. [2017] 86 taxmann.com 100 (Cal.)].

Grid connectivity charges: - The payment for the transmission of electricity through transmission lines could trigger Section 194C due to the carriage of goods aspect, although it is a contentious issue with differing judicial views.

Franchisee - Payment made by assessee-company, engaged in providing education and training for various preparatory examinations to its franchisees running education centers across country would not be covered by section 194C [CIT v. Career Launcher India Ltd. [2012] 20 taxmann.com 637/207 Taxman 28 (Delhi)].

Licence fee - Where assessee paid licence fee to IRCTC for granting contract of catering service without deducting tax at source and it has been held that it being a case of payment of licence fee by contractee to contractor, thus, section 194C would not apply [PCIT v. Hakmichand D & Sons [2018] 97 taxmann.com 584/258 Taxman 207 (SC)].

Lease financing transaction - Where assessee-company obtained certain vehicles on lease financing for use of its employees and lease finance company did not provide any particular work or service as to maintenance of vehicles or otherwise for purpose of usage of vehicles and only transaction entered into between assessee and lease financing company was to make payment of lease rentals due to lease financing company and car would be handed over to employee through assessee, no TDS was to be deducted u/s 194C on payment made by assessee towards lease rentals under such lease finance [CIT v. Texas Instruments India (P.) Ltd. [2021] 127 taxmann.com 59 (Kar.), SLP notice issued in CIT v. Texas Instruments India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 138 taxmann.com 18/287 Taxman 181 (SC)].

Supply of materials- Where assessee, engaged in supplying electricity, made payment against supply of materials included in composite contract for executing turnkey project, provisions of section 194C would not apply in respect of such payment for supply of materials [CIT v. Executive Engineer [2015] 61 taxmann.com 414/234 Taxman 267 (Kar.), SLP granted in CIT v. Executive Engineer [2016] 69 taxmann.com 450/239 Taxman 511 (SC)].

Transaction not considered as work- Where assessee placed order to print SIM scratch cards but had not supplied any material to manufacturer of card, transaction could not be treated as contract for carrying out work liable to TDS u/s 194C [CIT v. Spice Telecommunications (P.) Ltd. [2014] 46 taxmann.com 28/224 Taxman 180 (Kar.)].

Damages - Amount paid by sub-contractor to main contractor on account of extra costs that main contractor had to incur due to delay in completion of work by sub-contractor was not liable to TDS u/s 194C [CIT v. Karnavati Infrastructure (P.) Ltd. [2015] 54 taxmann.com 246/229 Taxman 241 (Guj.)].

Minimum guarantee payments - Where assessee entered into merchant agreement with various hotels for facilitating reservation/booking of hotel rooms through platform of assessee, however, assessee was merely compensating shortfall pursuant to agreement and no work had been carried out, therefore, assessee would not be liable for TDS under section 194C on minimum guarantee payments made to hotels. [Oravel Stays (P.) Ltd. v. Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax, Special Range-7, [2024] 159 taxmann.com 423 (Delhi - Trib.)]

Wastage could not be treated as making charges - Where assessee engaged in manufacturing of gold and silver jewellery issued certain quantity of gold to goldsmiths for making new ornaments but received back lesser quantity and balance was left with goldsmiths, since no payment or credit of any sum by way of cash, issue of cheque or draft or by any other mode was made to goldsmith, such wastage could not be treated as making charges given by assessee to goldsmith and provisions of section 194C would not be applicable to assessee for non-deduction of TDS on amount of such wastage. [P.R. Gold and Silver Craft v. Deputy Commissioner of Income-tax, [2022] 145 taxmann.com 112 (Chennai - Trib.)

External development charges (EDC) paid by assessee-society to development authority (GMADA), as per policy decision of government and not out of contractual obligations, would not attract section 194C. [Punjab IAS & PCS Officers House Building Society Ltd. v. Income-tax Officer, [2024] 158 taxmann.com 293 (Chandigarh - Trib.)]

Mathadi Contractors - The mandate of Sec. 194C is that the relationship of the person paying any sum to the person carrying out any work including the supply of labour should be in the nature of the principal to contractor. After anxiously examining the provision of Maharashtra mathadi act and Scheme framed under it, we are of the opinion that there is no contractual relationship as a principal and contractor between these assesses and Mathadi Board, but in fact, in pursuance of the provision of the Act as well as the scheme, both these assesses are bound to engage the labourers or the workers through the Mathadi Board. In our opinion, the interpretation given by both the authorities below to the provisions of the Maharashtra mathadi act is totally misplaced as Sec. 194C has no application when these assesses remits the payment in respect of the wages payable to the workers or labourers engaged through the Mathadi Board. [M/s Mulchandbhai Mafatlal Patel, Sangli V. Income Tax Officer (25 November 2014)( Pune Tribunal)], [Gokuldas Virjibhai & Company v. Income tax Officer, Ward 1(2), Sangli], [Jalaram Traders, Sangli V. Income Tax Officer (25 November 2014)]

Steam supply contract: Discusses the applicability of Section 194C to a steam supply contract, where the contractor uses its own instruments and manpower but utilizes facilities provided by the client. The contract for the supply of steam, given its nature of work involving the contractor's instruments and manpower at the client's location, falls within the purview of Section 194C.

Facility management services: Predominantly routine operation and maintenance services fall under Section 194C. However, where services involve substantial technical or professional input, Section 194J may apply.

Machining work on casting products provided by customers, such transactions qualify as "work" under Section 194C, as they involve processing materials supplied by the customer according to their specifications.
Customer contracts: Payments for the assignment of customer contracts do not fall under Section 194C as they do not constitute "work."

Contract Manufacturing on principal-to-principal basis: mere specifications-oriented manufacturing does not vitiate the nature of the contract for sale. If the contract manufacturer supplies goods to ICo on a principal-to-principal basis, where the title in the goods passes to ICo on delivery, Section 194C would not apply. This stance is further supported by the amendment to Section 194C by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2009, which clarifies that the section is triggered only where the works contract involves the purchase of raw material by the contractor from the customer.

Payments to Cooperative Societies- Payments made towards maintenance and other charges to a cooperative society do not result in any income for the society or its members, and thus, no withholding tax obligation arises under Section 194C. The relationship between members and the society is seen as mutual, and the payments are akin to members bearing their own expenses.

Payments to Farmers- Payments made to farmers for agricultural activities, where the income is treated as agricultural income and claimed as exempt under Section 10(1), may not trigger withholding tax obligations under Section 194C. The activity performed by the farmers may be regarded as a works contract, but since agricultural income is exempt from tax, the applicability of Section 194C becomes academic

Acquiring commercial rights to sell event tickets- Assessee acquired commercial rights to sell event tickets. Under such an agreement, the payment made by Assessee to Vendor for acquiring the right to sell tickets may not trigger withholding under Sections 194C, 194H, or 194J, provided that Assessee is only a ticketing partner and bears no responsibility for the event. Section 194C may not apply since the activity undertaken by Assessee does not qualify as “work” as per the definition under Section 194C.

Site erection under EPC contracts- Assessee made payments for site erection under EPC contracts. Payments towards erection charges under EPC contracts are subject to withholding under Section 194C as they fall within the definition of “work” for carrying out any work in pursuance of a contract. Even though the contract may involve technical services, it is primarily a works contract.

Bonus payments made to contracted labourers- Bonus payments are made to contracted laborers by Assessee. Section 194C triggers only when a payment is made for carrying out work and in pursuance to a contract between the parties. Voluntary payments made by the querist directly to the contractual laborers do not trigger Section 194C as they are not made in pursuance of a contract for carrying out work.

Contractual payments for manufacturing and sale agreements- withholding applicability on Contractual payments for manufacturing and sale agreements before and after the amendment by the Finance Act, 2009.
- Pre-amendment: If the arrangement is on a principal-to-principal basis, Section 194C may not apply.
- Post-amendment: If the manufacturer is required to purchase materials from the customer and the contract involves specifications and quality control by the customer, Section 194C may apply as the transaction may be considered as “work” under the amended definition.

Contract manufacturer uses raw materials provided by Contractee- Assessee Co sells raw materials to a contract manufacturer who then produces finished goods for Vendor Co, related to Assesseee Co. When the contract manufacturer uses raw materials provided by Assessee Co to manufacture goods as per Vendor Co’s specifications, it falls under Section 194C. However, if the manufacturer uses materials sourced from third parties, the arrangement may be considered a contract for sale rather than a work contract.
Annexure:
Understanding of Word/ Phrase of section 194C and its interpretation under case laws
‘ANY WORK’

Associated Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1993] 67 Taxman 347/201 ITR 435 (SC): 'Any work' means any work and not a works contract. 'Work' envisaged in the sub-section has a wide import and covers 'any work' which one or the other of the specified organisations can get carried out through a contractor under a contract. It further includes obtaining by any of such organisations supply, of labour under a contract with a contractor for carrying out its work which would have fallen outside the scope of work but for its specific inclusion in the sub-section.

Bombay Goods Transport Association v. CBDT [1994] 76 Taxman 334/210 ITR 136 (Bom.): The expression 'any work' used in section 194C means 'works contracts' and 'contracts for work', i.e., 'labour contracts' but not 'service contracts' or 'transport contracts'.
‘CARRYING OUT ANY WORK’

Birla Cement Works v.CBDT [1997] 95 Taxman 377 (Raj.): The expression 'carrying out any work' is the soul of section 194C and the applicability of the section depends upon the interpretation of this expression. The word 'any' is a word which excludes the limitation and qualification and can mean 'all', 'each' and 'every'. The meaning of this word given in the statute depends upon the context and the subject-matter of the statute and its generality can be restricted by the context in which it has been used. It has been used as a prefix to the word 'work' which means engagement in the performance of a task, duty or the likes. The term 'work' covers all forms of physical and mental exertions or both combined for the attainment of some object other than recreation or amusement. The dictionary meaning of the words 'carrying on' implies a repetition of acts.

Wadilal Dairy International Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2001] 118 Taxman 141/[2002] 81 ITD 238 (Pune - Trib.): The requirement of section 194C is that in order to attract the provisions, the assessee should have made payment to a contractor for carrying out any work, including supply of labour for carrying out any work. The expression 'contract for carrying out any work' implies that the contractor should have carried out such activities. The term 'carrying out' suggests an executory contract rather than a case of a mere supply or sale of goods. If a person engages the services of another and gives him a job of manufacturing goods or articles and for the purpose supplies him raw material, it would be a clear case of a contract of work. In such cases, the provisions of section 194C would undoubtedly be applicable. But, if on the other hand, a manufacturer, on his own, purchases material and manufactures product which he sells to the assessee - and it may be that such product might be customer-specific as per the requirement of the customer, it is still a case of a sale and not for carrying out any work. In such sale which is customer-specific, the fact that the goods manufactured are according to the requirement of the customer does not mean or imply that any work has been carried out on behalf of the contractee. The distinction between a sale and works contract is very significant particularly under the sales-tax laws. Before the introduction of tax on work contract, the sales-tax was levied on sales and it could not be levied on works contract. In sub-clause (b) of Board's Circular No. 681, dated 8-3-1991, it is stated that where the contractor undertakes to supply any articles or thing fabricated according to the specifications given by the Government or any other specified person and the property in such article or thing passes to the Government or such person only after such article or thing is delivered, the contract will be a contract for sale and as such outside the purview of section 194C. As per para (b), even in fabrication contracts if the property in the article passes to the Government or other person after its delivery, still it is a case of contract for sale. The fact that fabrication has been carried out as per specification given by the contractee is not considered to be relevant.
‘WORK’

Nitin M. Panchamiya v. Addl. CIT [2012] 19 taxmann.com 200/50 SOT 468/148 TTJ 96 (Mum.): The expression 'work' has not been defined for the purpose of section 194C. The normal meaning of the expression 'work' should, therefore, apply. By Explanation III(b) to section 194C, the Legislature only clarified that the expression 'work' shall also include broadcasting and telecasting including production of programmes or such broadcasting or telecasting. Therefore, the word 'work' would also include within its fold production of motion films or cinematographic films.

CIT v. Career Launcher India Ltd. [2012] 20 taxmann.com 637/207 Taxman 28/250 CTR 240 (Delhi): 'Work' did not include manufacturing or supplying a product according to the requirement upon specification of a customer by using raw materials purchased from a person other than such customer; as such a contract is a contract for sale.

CIT v. Karnataka Power Transmission Corpn. Ltd. [2012] 21 taxmann.com 473/208 Taxman 73 (Kar.): The word 'work' did not include manufacturing or supplying a product according to the requirement and specification of a customer by using raw materials purchased from a person other than such customer as such a contract is a contract for sale.

ITO v. Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd. [2014] 45 taxmann.com 124/64 SOT 138 (Mum.): The word 'work' stands defined under Explanation III to section 194C in an inclusive manner to include provision of certain specified services, viz., advertising, catering, broadcasting and telecasting, carriage of goods or passengers, etc. The maintenance work would, therefore, clearly fall within the ambit of 'work' as defined under section 194C. Again, the same may involve work of some technical nature or the persons carrying it out as being technically qualified. It is, in fact, nobody's case that the same could be performed by persons who are not technically qualified or skilled. But, as explained by the Tribunal in Tata AIG General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. ITO [2011] 43 SOT 215/[2010] 8 taxmann.com 158 (Mum. - Trib.), it is the nature of the work for which the payment is made and not to whom it is, which is relevant.

Dy. CIT v. Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd. [2015] 61 taxmann.com 138/38 ITR (Trib.) 636 (Mum.): The expression 'work' in section 194C includes broadcasting, telecasting and production of TV programmes.
CIT v. UTV Entertainment Television Ltd. [2017] 88 taxmann.com 214 (Bom.): The work of subtitling will be covered by the definition of "work" in clause (iv) of Explanation to section 194C.
‘WORK CONTRACTS’

CIT v. Bangalore District Co-operative Milk Producers Societies Union Ltd. [2013] 36 taxmann.com 120/357 ITR 676/261 CTR 442 (Kar.): The explanation 'works contract' has a definite legal connotation. What is stated in the section 194C(1) is for 'carrying out any works' between the contractor and specified person. The work is also defined to exclude the situation where the material is not supplied by the assessee. The fact that in clause (a), the definition of work as amended subsequently, was not in the statutory book for the relevant years in question, would not be of consequence because of the ratio laid down in CIT v. Karnataka Power Transmission Corpn. Ltd. [2012] 208 Taxman 73/21 taxmann.com 473 (Kar.).The definition is clarificatory in nature.

In State of Himachal Pradesh v. Associated Hotels of India Ltd. [1972] 29 STC 474, the Supreme Court observed that where the principal objective of work undertaken by the payee of the price is not the transfer of a chattel qua chattel, contract is of work and labour. The test is whether or not the work and labour bestowed end in anything that can properly become the subject of sale; neither the ownership of the materials nor the value of skill and labour as compared with the value of the materials is conclusive although such matters may be taken into consideration in determining, in the circumstances of a particular case, whether the contract is, in substance, one of work and labour or one for the sale of a chattel. A building contract or a contract under which a movable is fixed to another chattel or on the land, where the intention plainly is not to sell the article but to improve the land or the chattel and the consideration is not for the transfer of the chattel, but for the labour and work done and the material furnished, the contract will be one of work and labour.
‘Sub contract’

From a perusal of section 194C, it is obvious that a contractor for the purpose of these provisions would be any person who enters Into a contract with the Central or any State Government, any local authority, and corporation established by or under a Central, State Or Provincial Act, any company or any co-operative society for carrying out any work including the supply of labour for carrying out any work and a sub-contractor would mean any person who enters into a contract for carrying out, the whole Or part of the work undertaken by the contractor under the contract with any of the authorities named above or for supply whether wholly Or partly any labour which the contractor has undertaken to supply in terms of his contract with any of the aforesaid authorities. [UTO v. Rama Nand & Co. terms (1987) 163 ITR 702, 704 (HP)]
